title: 'End ongoing violations of Orang Asli land rights in Pahang – 19 NGOs
body: 'We, the undersigned civil society organisations and individuals, are deeply concerned by the situation confronting the Orang Asli of Pahang in general, and of the communities of Tasek Bera in particular, who are facing eviction, harassment and arrest and are being treated as a scapegoat for ongoing deforestation. Violations in Tasek Bera In June 2026, about 20 Orang Asli villages in the Tasek Bera area received eviction notices from the Pahang Forestry Department, ordering them to vacate their settlements and farmland. These kampungs, including Kampung Kuala Serting, Kampung Lubuk Tiang, Kampung Tambangan, Kampung Lenguin, Kampung Gakuyah, Kampung Pathir, Kampung Limbahan, Kampung Mahang, Kampung Ibam and Kampung Buloh Nipis, lie within the Tasek Bera permanent forest reserve (hutan simpan kekal). In response, the communities acted collectively, erecting blockades to protect their customary lands and monitoring activities within their territories. On 14 September, officers from the Pahang State Forestry Department and Department of Wildlife arrived at Kampung Pathir, stating their intention to conduct land surveying. The communities refused them entry pending a resolution on the eviction notices, with Tok Batin Amir Noor Tan of Kampung Pathir calling for the eviction notices to be withdrawn. This standoff escalated, resulting in the arrest of five Orang Asli, four of them women, on the same day. They were subsequently released on 16 September. - Sign up for Aliran's free daily email updates or weekly newsletters or both - Make a one-off donation to Persatuan Aliran Kesedaran Negara (ALIRAN), Maybank a/c 507246118995 or CIMB a/c 8004240948 - Make a regular pledge or periodic auto-donation to Aliran - Become an Aliran member Another similar incident involving police and communities within Tasek Bera also took place in Kampung Kuala Serting on 23 September. These recent developments are not an isolated case and form part of a growing trend of land grabs in Pahang. For example, outside Tasek Bera, on 9 February, 21 Orang Asli villagers from Kampung Jemeri in Rompin, Pahang, were detained by police following a complaint from a company claiming rights to develop land allegedly owned by the sultan of Pahang. According to a community statement, the sultan had [allegedly] obtained title to the 718-hectare oil palm plantation, developed by Orang Asli smallholders, less than a month earlier, on 26 January. The land in question forms part of the traditional territories of Jakun smallholders who had opened their smallholdings there 10-13 years ago. Orang Asli not driving deforestation Since early 2026, we have observed the development of a narrative in Pahang portraying the Orang Asli as groups that are scheming with outsiders to convert forest reserves into agricultural land. For example, while the above events were occurring in Tasek Bera, mainstream and state media repeatedly circulated claims that more than 7,000 hectares of forest within the Tasek Bera Ramsar site, which spans 38,446 hectares, had been illegally converted. This conversion was attributed to six Orang Asli families who allegedly used outsiders to exploit customary land rights in carrying out the encroachment. This narrative fails to accurately depict the drivers of deforestation in the state. A recent article by RimbaWatch found that at least 72,000 hectares of forest are under threat in Pahang, driven primarily by the expansion of monoculture industrial timber plantations in forest reserves, a programme supported by both the state and federal governments. Measured against this scale, traditional forest utilisation carried out by Orang Asli communities is minor. Yet it is their communities, not state and corporate drivers of deforestation, that are being singled out and blamed. Orang Asli traditional territories have existed for generations, predating independence and their later gazettement as timber production areas. Research has continuously shown that safeguarded Indigenous territories exhibit remarkable ecological resilience and biodiversity outcomes. Arrests of Orang Asli community members, ongoing harassment and the undue stress of receiving eviction notices or discovering that their land now belongs to outsiders all point to a troubling reality: as rights to their traditional territories are denied, the Orang Asli in Pahang are becoming outsiders on their own territories and scapegoated as drivers of widespread deforestation. Apex courts’ consistent rulings The Federal Court and Court of Appeal have repeatedly recognised that Orang Asli possess native customary land rights – a form of proprietary right protected under Article 13 of the Federal Constitution, provided a substantial connection to the land in question can be proven [Rosli Jendut & Ors v Agrobest (M) Sdn Bhd & Ors (2026)]. These rights pre-date both the Aboriginal Peoples Act 1954 and the National Land Code, and do not depend on any document of title. The rights are not limited to settlement areas. As the Federal Court in Rosli Jendut makes clear, these rights also extend to lands which are central to the Orang Asli’s cultural way of life, such as tombstones and grave sites. As such, despite the lack of gazettement and formal documents of title, the proprietary rights of Orang Asli communities in Tasek Bera over their traditional territories should be recognised and respected according to the Federal Court. Call to action The gaps between the judiciary and the executive are glaring and deeply concerning. While the courts have, time and again, affirmed the proprietary rights of the Orang Asli to their traditional territories, this recognition is not reflected by executive action. Communities like the Orang Asli in Tasek Bera, while actively fighting to protect their territories, are bearing the cost of this disconnect through evictions, arrests and the destruction of their lands. We urge the federal government to intervene immediately to safeguard the rights and wellbeing of the Orang Asli, as recognised by our Federal Courts and the Constitution. We call for an end to the misleading and negative portrayal of the Orang Asli community. Furthermore, we call for the following measures. - The Pahang state government must withdraw all eviction notices issued to the Orang Asli communities in Pahang, particularly those grounded solely on the claim that the communities are residing within permanent forest reserves. - The Pahang state government and their agencies must conduct genuine free, prior and informed consent consultation with affected communities for any decisions that will affect them, in line with Malaysia’s commitments under the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP). - Suhakam must conduct an independent inquiry into the conduct of the Tasek Bera enforcement operations, and the findings made public and acted upon by the federal and Pahang state government without delay, vis-a-vis recommendations made in the 2013 National Inquiry on the Land Rights of Indigenous Peoples in Malaysia being adopted and implemented. - The Pahang state government and its agencies (eg Jakoa) must accelerate and make transparent the gazettement of Orang Asli traditional territories, with clear timelines for the villages still pending survey. - The federal government must halt the ongoing amendment process of the Orang Asli Act 1954 until legally binding recognition of traditional territories is guaranteed. Endorsed by the following organisations / Disokong oleh organisasi berikut: - RimbaWatch - Centre for Orang Asli Concerns (COAC) - Save Rivers - Pertubuhan Wanita Orang Asal Malaysia (PWOAM) - Alliance of River Three (Art!) - Gabungan Darurat Iklim Malaysia - Saya Anak Bangsa Malaysia (SABM) - University of Malaya Association of New Youth (Umany） - Amnesty International Malaysia - Greenpeace Malaysia - Teoh Beng Hock Association for Democratic Advancement (TBH-ADA) - SeDarjat - Persatuan Kesedaran Komuniti Selangor (Empower) - Parti Sosialis Malaysia (PSM) - Gabungan Marhaen - Kemban Kolektif - Greater Equitable Measures (Gem) – Malaysia - Center to Combat Corruption and Cronyism (C4 Center) - Centre for Independent Journalism (CIJ) upan rakyat - Galakkan pembangunan saksama, lestari serta tangani krisis alam sekitar - Raikan kerencaman dan keterangkuman - Selamatkan demokrasi dan angkatkan keluhuran undang-undang - Lawan rasuah dan kronisme Endorsed by the following individuals / Disokong oleh individu berikut: The views expressed in Aliran's media statements and the NGO statements we have endorsed reflect Aliran's official stand. title: 'Permohonan Shamsul Iskandar untuk dapat pasport secara kekal diketahui 8 Disember
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR - Mahkamah Sesyen di sini menetapkan 8 Disember ini bagi memutuskan permohonan Datuk Seri Shamsul Iskandar Mohd. Akin untuk mendapatkan semula pasportnya secara kekal bagi memudahkan beliau menghadiri beberapa program di luar negara.  Hakim Suzana Hussin menetapkan tarikh itu selepas mendengar permohonan peguam Yusmadi Yusoff yang mewakili pemohon yang juga bekas Setiausaha Politik Kanan Perdana Menteri.  Pasport tersebut berada dalam simpanan mahkamah sebagai syarat jaminan tambahan selepas beliau didakwa atas lima pertuduhan rasuah.  Pada prosiding hari ini, Yusmadi memaklumkan bahawa permohonan bagi mendapatkan pasport secara kekal, difailkan pada 30 September lalu.  Menurut beliau, anak guamnya juga memohon pasport secara sementara bagi membolehkan beliau menghadiri program di Frankfurt dan London, bulan ini.  Bagaimanapun, Timbalan Pendakwa Raya Julaila Jamaludin membantah permohonan Shamsul Iskandar untuk mendapatkan pasportnya secara kekal atas alasan dokumen yang dikemukakan hanya berupa surat jemputan dan terdapat perbincangan yang boleh dijalankan secara dalam talian.  Bagaimanapun, Julaila tidak membantah permohonan Shamsul Iskandar untuk mendapatkan pasport secara sementara.  Suzana kemudian membenarkan pasport Shamsul Iskandar diberikan secara sementara mulai hari ini dan perlu diserahkan semula kepada mahkamah pada atau sebelum 16 Oktober ini.  Selain itu, mahkamah memerintahkan pihak pendakwaan memfailkan afidavit balasan terhadap permohonan Shamsul Iskandar bagi mendapatkan pasport secara kekal pada atau sebelum 19 Oktober ini.  Menerusi afidavit bagi menyokong permohonannya, Shamsul Iskandar berkata, beliau memerlukan pasportnya untuk perjalanan ke empat buah negara iaitu Frankfurt, London, Ireland dan Bosnia Herzegovina, dalam masa terdekat.  Berdasarkan dokumen yang diperoleh antara program yang dihadiri ialah pesta buku, sidang kemuncak dan lawatan kerja penglibatan perniagaan strategik.  Katanya, beliau berhasrat untuk ke Frankfurt, Jerman bagi menghadiri pesta buku bertajuk 'Frankfurt Book Fair' yang dianjurkan oleh Rex Education dan dijadualkan berlangsung 7 Oktober hingga 11 November.  "Berdasarkan penglibatan saya dengan Akademi Kepimpinan Masyarakat Madani, penyertaan dalam pesta buku tersebut bertujuan untuk memupuk sinergi antara organisasi serta memberikan manfaat bersama kepada kedua-dua entiti," katanya.  Sementara itu, bagi lawatan di London, Shamsul Iskandar memaklumkan beliau mendaftar untuk Sidang Kemuncak AlBaraka kelima bertajuk Ethics in Action: Rebuilding Foundations and Advancing the Global Impact of the Islamic Economy' yang akan berlangsung dari 13 Oktober hingga 14 Oktober ini.  Menurutnya, objektif utama sidang kemuncak tersebut adalah untuk memberi tumpuan kepada pengukuhan asas etika yang autentik bagi institusi kewangan Islam dan institusi bukan kewangan, sistem tadbir urus serta amalan pasaran.  Dalam pada itu, perjalanan ke Ireland dijadual bermula 27 November hingga 4 Disember ini bagi memenuhi jemputan Perbincangan Lanjutan Mengenai Strategi Perniagaan di negara itu.  Selain itu, beliau turut dijemput ke Bosnia Herzegovina pada November dan Disember ini untuk menghadiri beberapa siri perbincangan kedua-dua negara dalam pelbagai lapangan termasuk keusahawanan, pembangunan ekonomi dan transformasi sosial.  Justeru beliau memohon supaya pasport antarabangsanya dilepaskan secara kekal daripada tarikh perintah mahkamah bagi memudahkannya melakukan perjalanan ke luar negara.  Shamsul Iskandar, 51, didakwa atas dua pertuduhan bersetuju menerima suapan untuk dirinya, iaitu wang tunai RM140,000 daripada ahli perniagaan Tei Jiann Cheing atau turut dikenali sebagai Albert Tei sebagai dorongan membantu syarikat milik Albert Tei untuk mendapatkan kelulusan lesen penerokaan mineral di Sabah.  Dia turut didakwa atas dua lagi pertuduhan iaitu memperoleh untuk dirinya satu suapan berupa kelengkapan perabot dan barangan elektrik bernilai RM14,580.03 dan RM22,249 daripada individu sama bagi tujuan sama.  Kesalahan itu didakwa dilakukan di premis di Jalan Medang Serai, Bukit Bandaraya; di tempat letak kereta sebuah hotel di Jalan Sultan Hishamuddin di sini; serta di Jalan P14A 1/1, Presint 14, Putrajaya, antara 7 Disember 2023 dan 31 Januari 2024, serta antara 24 November 2023 dan 5 Mac 2024.  Shamsul Iskandar turut didakwa atas satu pertuduhan memperoleh suapan berjumlah RM64,924 yang dimasukkan ke dalam akaun CIMB Bank milik Rahmalidya Buyong bagi tujuan pembayaran penyewaan sebuah rumah di Jalan Medang Serai, Bukit Bandaraya, di sini, daripada Albert Tei bagi membantu syarikat miliknya mendapatkan kelulusan lesen penerokaan mineral di Sabah. - MalaysiaGazette

title: 'Cover Story: Banks shift tokenisation into higher gear
body: 'This article first appeared in Wealth, The Edge Malaysia Weekly on September 28, 2026 - October 4, 2026 Tokenisation, the act of representing an asset or claim as a token on a distributed ledger or blockchain, has remained under the radar among local financial institutions. Until recently. The catalyst, market observers say, came from Bank Negara Malaysia, when it launched the Digital Asset Innovation Hub (DAIH) in June 2025 and published its discussion paper on asset tokenisation in the Malaysian financial sector in October 2025. The public feedback window for the discussion paper closed on March 1, 2026, and Bank Negara hosted its third Asset Tokenisation Industry Working Group session in August this year. The discussion paper states that proof-of-concepts and live pilots will be conducted in a controlled environment through the DAIH this year, with testing expected to continue into 2027, alongside the compilation and publication of findings and the evaluation of key insights. Three banks have launched initiatives under the DAIH. The banks are under CIMB Group Holdings Bhd (KL:CIMB); Standard Chartered Bank Malaysia Bhd (Standard Chartered Malaysia), together with Capital A Bhd (KL:CAPITALA); and Malayan Banking Bhd (KL:MAYBANK). Chu Kok Wei, CEO of group wholesale banking and corporate treasurer at CIMB Group, says Malaysian banks are not the earliest to embrace the technology, but they have been moving fast recently. “We might be the country that’s moving at the fastest speed in Southeast Asia in the last one year, based on my observation, by looking at all the stakeholders and our experience and conversation with regulators,” he says. His observation coincides with the findings of HSBC’s Redefining Treasury in Asia Pacific 2026: Voices of Treasury report, published on Sept 17. The report notes that Malaysia stands out as the most enthusiastic market in the region on digital currency adoption, with 50% of respondents saying they were very likely to use digital currencies in the next two years, far higher than the regional average of 19%. Digital currency is tokenised money, which can take the form of tokenised deposits, stablecoins or central bank digital currency. Some 42% of respondents in Malaysia also say digital assets in treasury are high risk, broadly in line with the regional average of 44%, even as they see both opportunity and complexity. The biggest benefits of tokenisation, which is underpinned by blockchain or distributed ledger technology, are greater treasury efficiency (73%) and enhanced liquidity management (50%). “The challenge now is for market infrastructure to catch up to the demand,” says Anand Mukati, head of global payments solutions at HSBC Malaysia. Elsewhere, global banks in developed markets such as the US have been moving fast in tokenisation by adopting blockchain technology. In its Tokenisation 2030: Wall Street On-Chain report published in June, US-based multinational bank Citigroup points out that tokenisation is moving towards operational reality. The Depository Trust and Clearing Corporation (DTCC), the US industry-owned clearing house and central securities depository, received regulatory clearance in late 2025 to offer a tokenisation service for DTCC-custodied assets, with a three-year pilot planned for late 2026. The New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) announced plans for a tokenised securities platform by late 2026, subject to regulatory approval, which would enable 24/7 trading of US-listed equities and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) with near-instant settlement and stablecoin-based funding. Nasdaq has also received the Securities and Exchange Commission’s (SEC) approval to enable certain stocks and ETFs to be issued, traded and settled in tokenised form. “These organisations are not crypto-native firms pushing blockchain, but some of the oldest and largest financial institutions adopting new infrastructure,” according to Citi. On Sept 17, the SEC unveiled its long-awaited exemption that will allow companies to offer trading in blockchain-based or “tokenised” stocks and other securities. Four days later, the European Central Bank launched preparatory work to invest a small portion of its own fund in tokenised securities, enabling it to gain practical experience as an investor and build institutional expertise in the use of distributed ledger technology in financial markets. The world is moving fast. Completed and ongoing initiatives When Khazanah Nasional Bhd completed its RM100 million tokenised sukuk pilot project in mid-May, CIMB acted as its sole principal adviser, sole lead arranger and sole facility agent. About three months later, the bank took that experience further, completing the country’s first pilot testing of the settlement of tokenised sukuk using tokenised deposits in a controlled environment. For comparison, Khazanah’s tokenised sukuk pilot project settled the exchange of sukuk on the blockchain, but its cash transactions were conducted through traditional banking channels in fiat currency instead of tokenised deposits. Put simply, a tokenised deposit is a form of digital money that is transferred and settled on a secure blockchain or distributed ledger, rather than through traditional payment infrastructure such as PayNet’s Real-time Retail Payments Platform (RPP) or Bank Negara’s RENTAS+. In an interview with Wealth, CIMB’s Chu says the bank’s pilot project represents a meaningful breakthrough, with CIMB Islamic Bank Bhd issuing RM1.68 billion in sukuk under its existing RM10 billion senior sukuk wakalah programme, across tenors of five, seven, 10 and 15 years. Of the total issuance, RM1.38 billion was represented in tokenised form and subscribed by 12 institutional investors. Both legs of the transaction — CIMB’s tokenised sukuk and the tokenised deposits used to pay for them — were settled on the bank’s own blockchain, CIMB Blockchain Connect. “Khazanah’s tokenised sukuk pilot project was RM100 million with a one-year tenure. We were part of the consortium that arranged the transaction. We took that learning and, in less than five months, we printed our own transaction of RM1.68 billion, out of which RM1.38 billion was tokenised up to 15 years. “This progression is important. That means we are moving from a pilot size transaction to a market size transaction backed by real investor demand,” he says. Institutions that subscribed to CIMB’s tokenised sukuk include sovereign wealth funds, pension funds, insurers, corporates and asset managers, reflecting market confidence in the programme. “We like to think that we have built enough momentum for this to carry forward,” says Chu. The DAIH’s official website lists the initiatives of the three banks. CIMB focuses on tokenised deposits for the settlement of tokenised securities, Maybank on tokenised deposits for payments, and Standard Chartered Malaysia and Capital A on ringgit stablecoins for business-to-business (B2B) settlement. Maybank also played a leading role as joint lead manager, custodian and primary subscriber of Khazanah's RM100 million tokenised sukuk pilot project. In an email response, Maybank global head of markets structuring and quants Rivai Tan says the bank has explored and tested use cases within its own environment to accelerate learning. “This led to initiatives spanning tokenised deposits, near real-time cross-border payments and tokenised investment solution pilots,” he says. Among the initiatives Maybank is involved in is a RM1 million pilot transaction for tokenised supply chain financing, announced on Aug 20 and aimed at enhancing transparency and resilience across supply chain ecosystems. The transaction was carried out in partnership with Virtual Economy Technology Sdn Bhd (V System) via its tokenisation platform, NexA. V System is a participant in the Securities Commission Malaysia’s regulatory sandbox to pilot innovative blockchain-based solutions. Earlier, on March 30, the bank successfully completed the first transaction of its tokenised deposits and cross-border payments with energy infrastructure company Yinson Holdings Bhd (KL:YINSON). Tokenised securities and deposits are programmable, which is where smart contracts come into play. A smart contract is code on a blockchain that automatically carries out the terms of an agreement when conditions are met, without human intervention. Chu says smart contracts can be used for market events. For instance, where a bond or sukuk pays a coupon every six months, the profit can be distributed automatically via the distributed ledger. “All these are baby steps that we are taking, from the primary market to secondary, and eventually it covers even redemptions,” he says. Tokenised securities can be fractionalised, which opens up the possibility of tokenised bonds and sukuk becoming easily accessible to retail investors at a much lower amount. But Chu says tokenisation and blockchain are merely a technological enabler; further democratisation of bonds and sukuk would require changes in rules and regulations. “We all need to kind of contain our excitement about how tokenisation enables retail participation for now. It provides a platform, but suitability for investors, fair disclosure [of information] and all other relevant processes have to be continuously assessed by the regulators,” he says. Interoperability between blockchains, and between the new and old systems Against such a backdrop, tokenisation initiatives undertaken by local banks are based on the “digital twin” concept, which means the on-chain token mirrors the traditional legal records rather than replacing them. “From a legal sense, digital twin means the whole process of the issuance of CIMB sukuk follows existing rules and regulations and contract. The original contract remains valid, while the digital token is only a replica. In this case, you don’t need to answer what is the relationship of the replica and the underlying assets,” says Chu. However, the country’s rules and regulations will need to change if financial services were to move fully onto the blockchain, which is one of the challenges in tokenisation. Chu says other challenges include interoperability, which means the deployment of digital tokens across the different blockchains of different banks. However, he says CIMB prefers to focus on something else: the interoperability between the new technology, which is the blockchain, and the existing ones, especially in the bond market. “This is much more important as bonds and sukuk are an established asset class with a total value of more than RM2 trillion in the system. There are many 30-year bonds out there and they start to worry about what happens if all these are going to be tokenised,” he says. Maybank’s Tan agrees that beyond technology and process design, the successful deployment of tokenisation also depends on many other factors, including interoperability, regulatory alignment and broader industry adoption. From a practical perspective, a key challenge lies in integrating tokenised solutions into existing systems, processes and operating models, he adds. This means a bank needs to stay forward-looking and rethink workflows from the ground up, including what should be retained, rebuilt, simplified or, in some cases, fundamentally redesigned to realise the full benefits of tokenisation. “Realising the full potential of tokenisation will require close collaboration among regulators, financial institutions and technology providers to establish common standards and trusted market infrastructure,” says Tan. Standard Chartered Malaysia’s Mushahid Syed adds that developing digital infrastructure that offers accessible, cost-effective and instant alternative wholesale payments is key for a trading nation like Malaysia, with its strong small and medium enterprise base. There is little doubt that tokenisation, underpinned by blockchain technology, will make banking and financial services more efficient and effective when it matures. Workflows, organisational structures and the content of certain jobs may evolve. Changes are already afoot. “An example I always tell everyone is that we are now using iPhone 18, which has evolved significantly from its first version. The same applies to the evolution of the financial services industry and the role of people working in it,” says Chu. Save by subscribing to us for your print and/or digital copy. title: 'Bursa Malaysia dibuka tinggi, jejaki peningkatan di Wall Street
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR, 5 Oktober: Bursa Malaysia dibuka lebih tinggi pada Isnin, menjejaki kenaikan Wall Street berikutan pertumbuhan gaji Amerika Syarikat (AS) yang lebih perlahan, meredakan jangkaan kenaikan kadar faedah serta-merta oleh Rizab Persekutuan (Fed) AS. Pada 9.10 pagi, FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI (FBM KLCI) meningkat 5.01 mata atau 0.31 peratus kepada 1,635.88 berbanding paras 1,630.87 ketika ditutup pada Jumaat. Indeks utama itu dibuka 2.55 mata lebih tinggi kepada 1,633.42. Sentimen pasaran secara keseluruhan positif dengan kaunter untung mengatasi kaunter rugi sebanyak 224 berbanding 158, sebanyak 337 kaunter tidak berubah, 2,054 tidak diniagakan dan 24 digantung dagangan. Jumlah dagangan berjumlah 206.30 juta saham bernilai RM98.78 juta. Naib Presiden Penyelidikan Ekuiti Rakuten Trade Sdn Bhd, Thong Pak Leng berkata hasil bon 10 tahun AS kekal tinggi pada paras 5.28 peratus manakala harga minyak mentah Brent ditutup pada US$102.25 setong, menjadikan sentimen pasaran sensitif terhadap kadar faedah dan perkembangan di Asia Barat. “Di Hong Kong, Indeks Hang Seng susut di bawah paras 24,000 berikutan penyusutan saham sektor kewangan dan teknologi. “Di pasaran tempatan, susulan penutupan lebih tinggi FBM KLCI pada Jumaat lepas, kami menjangkakan kestabilan sementara dalam julat 1,625-1,635 hari ini, dengan aktiviti pembelian saham pada harga rendah memberikan sedikit sokongan di sebalik sentimen pasaran yang berhati-hati,” katanya kepada Bernama. Saham wajaran tinggi menyaksikan Maybank, Public Bank, CIMB dan Tenaga Nasional menambah empat sen masing-masing kepada RM10.06, RN4.70, RM7.69, dan RM13.00, manakala IHH Healthcare berkurangan enam sen kepada RM7.74. Bagi saham aktif, VS Industry menambah tiga sen kepada 32 sen, Notion VTec naik empat sen kepada 74.5 sen, GB Bond meningkat setengah sen kepada 23.5 sen, SFP Tech menokok satu sen kepada 28.5 sen, manakala Dagang NeXchange tidak berubah pada 51.5 sen. Antara saham paling untung, Samaiden naik 19 sen kepada RM3.03, UWC meningkat 16 sen kepada RM7.73, Critical Holdings menokok 15 sen kepada RM2.61, Mi Technovation melonjak sembilan sen kepada RM5.30, dan Solarvest mengukuh lapan sen kepada RM4.25. Nestle mendahului saham paling rugi, susut 32 sen to RM89.20, manakala Vitrox merosot 14 sen kepada RM10.32, Kobay Technology berkurangan 12 sen kepada RM2.18, Kelington menguncup lima sen kepada RM8.58, dan YTL Power International turun empat sen kepada RM5.64. Di papan indeks, Indeks FBM Mid 70 menambah 28.14 mata kepada 17,510.07, Indeks FBM Emas meningkat 33.81 mata kepada 12,204.38, Indeks FBM Top 100 naik 32.24 mata kepada 11,989.92, Indeks FBM Emas Syariah bertambah 22.28 mata kepada 12,082.60, manakala Indeks FBM ACE meningkat 31.41 mata kepada 5,560.87. Mengikut sektor, Indeks Produk dan Perkhidmatan Perindustrian naik 0.59 mata kepada 179.11, Indeks Tenaga naik 2.57 mata kepada 835.60, Indeks Perkhidmatan Kewangan meningkat 97.59 mata kepada 19,138.10, manakala Indeks Perladangan melonjak 2.23 mata kepada 9,058.78. – Bernama

title: 'Bursa Malaysia Gains on Wall Street Lead as Weak US Payrolls Temper Fed Rate Hike Expectations - MCI Group
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 5 — Bursa Malaysia opened higher on Monday, tracking Wall Street’s gains after softer US payroll growth eased expectations of an immediate Federal Reserve rate increase. At 9.10 am, the FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI (FBM KLCI) rose 5.01 points, or 0.31 per cent, to 1,635.88 from last Friday’s close of 1,630.87. The index opened 2.55 points higher at 1,633.42. On the broader market, gainers surpassed losers 224 to 158, with 337 counters unchanged, 2,054 untraded and 24 suspended. Turnover stood at 206.30 million shares worth RM98.78 million. Rakuten Trade Sdn Bhd vice-president of equity research Thong Pak Leng said the US 10-year yield remained elevated at 5.28 per cent and Brent crude oil settled at US$102.25 per barrel, keeping sentiment sensitive to interest rates and West Asia developments. “Over in Hong Kong, the Hang Seng Index slipped below 24,000 as financial and technology shares weakened. “Back home, following FBM KLCI’s higher close last Friday, we anticipate tentative stabilisation within 1,625-1,635 today, with bargain hunting offering some support amid a cautious market undertone,” he told Bernama. Among the heavyweights, Maybank, Public Bank, CIMB and Tenaga Nasional gained four sen each to RM10.06, RN4.70, RM7.69, and RM13.00, while IHH Healthcare decreased six sen to RM7.74. In active trade, VS Industry added three sen to 32 sen, Notion VTec increased four sen to 74.5 sen, GB Bond inched up half-a-sen to 23.5 sen, SFP Tech gained a sen to 28.5 sen, while Dagang NeXchange was flat at 51.5 sen. Among the top gainers, Samaiden put on 19 sen to RM3.03, UWC was 16 sen firmer at RM7.73, Critical Holdings perked up 15 sen to RM2.61, Mi Technovation strengthened nine sen to RM5.30, and Solarvest advanced eight sen to RM4.25. Nestle led the decliners, falling 32 sen to RM89.20, while Vitrox eased 14 sen to RM10.32, Kobay Technology was 12 sen lower at RM2.18, Kelington shed five sen to RM8.58, and YTL Power International edged down four sen to RM5.64. On the index board, the FBM Mid 70 Index gained 28.14 points to 17,510.07, the FBM Emas Index appreciated 33.81 points to 12,204.38, the FBM Top 100 Index widened 32.24 points to 11,989.92, the FBM Emas Shariah Index advanced 22.28 points to 12,082.60, and the FBM ACE Index improved 31.41 points to 5,560.87. Sector-wise, the Industrial Products and Services Index inched up 0.59 of-a-point to 179.11, the Energy Index gained 2.57 points to 835.60, the Financial Services Index jumped 97.59 points to 19,138.10, and the Plantation Index gained 2.23 points to 9,058.78.

Tak seperti warna lain yang sering dikenali dengan tanggapan yang lebih positif, warna merah seringkali disalah erti. 

“Ala, warna merah kan boleh melambangkan keberanian dan keyakinan? Positif lah tu?”

Betul, tapi tak mencukupi untuk membuatkan ramai orang ubah persepsi terhadap warna ini. Jadi, untuk mengubah pandangan kita, jom tonton video ini sampai habis.

Menerusi video jenama yang dibawakan oleh CIMB ini jelas menunjukkan gambaran yang warna merah BOLEH jadi positif dan beri impak besar dalam diri kita.

Ia bukan saja menampilkan keberanian, malah ia juga memberi kita semangat dan keyakinan untuk terus maju ke hadapan, sama ada untuk mengejar impian, merebut peluang, mengatasi cabaran ataupun sekadar untuk terus melangkah.

Bagi CIMB, untuk terus maju ke hadapan, ia hanya perlu bermula dengan satu pilihan iaitu untuk terus berjalan.

CIMB yang juga sinonim dengan warna merah turut memberi kita jaminan yang mereka akan sentiasa menyokong kita, memudahkan perjalanan dan membantu merealisasikan impian. 

Jadi, korang yang tengah membaca ni perlu ingat dan tanam dalam fikiran, warna merah sebenarnya boleh memberi impak positif dalam kehidupan harian kita. 

Sebagai jenama yang juga mempunyai warna merah sebagai identiti mereka, CIMB berjanji yang mereka akan sentiasa ada bersama kita untuk terus memacu ke hadapan.

title: 'CIMB IB says Malaysia could widen corporate tax base for Budget 2027, cut old deductions
body: 'CIMB IB says Malaysia could widen corporate tax base for Budget 2027, cut old deductions KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 5): Malaysia could widen its corporate tax base by reviewing special and double deductions that have been in place for two to three decades, and remove deductions that no longer serve their original purpose, said CIMB Investment Bank. CIMB IB said, citing KPMG senior adviser on tax policy Dr Verrinderjeet Singh during a discussion, that the removal of selected deductions could lead to the government collecting more revenue while creating room for a lower headline corporate tax rate. “His [Verrinderjeet] proposal is selective: investment incentives remain important for attracting businesses, but their benefits need closer scrutiny. He links Malaysia’s shift towards outcome-based incentives to its response to Global Minimum Tax,” said CIMB IB. It added, “Their effectiveness will depend on monitoring whether investors deliver the intended economic benefits”. Malaysia’s headline corporate income tax rate is currently 24%, but the amount of tax companies ultimately pay is also affected by deductions, exemptions and investment incentives. On major tax changes, CIMB IB said Malaysia is unlikely to introduce new tax changes in Budget 2027, with stronger collection from existing taxes and a wider tax base offering the main scope for raising government revenue. The government is expected to focus on improving tax collection, particularly by bringing more businesses into the tax net and identifying income that is not fully reported. Smaller businesses are likely to offer more room for additional collections, as larger companies are already more visible to the tax authorities, said CIMB IB. “His central message was that stronger collection and targeted refinements to existing taxes offer the main near-term revenue opportunities. Against a continued focus on cost-of-living support and the social agenda, he expects few substantial tax changes in the coming budget,” said CIMB IB. E-invoicing could help identify unreported taxable activity, although smaller businesses face additional compliance and technology costs. CIMB IB said Veerinderjeet expects participation to broaden as economic conditions improve. CIMB IB also sees scope for greater use of data analytics by the Inland Revenue Board (IRB) and Customs to identify businesses and income outside the existing tax net. On indirect taxes, CIMB IB said Veerinderjeet does not expect the goods and services tax (GST) to return in Budget 2027. Instead, the focus is likely to remain on improving the existing sales and service tax (SST). SST is estimated to cover about 78% to 80% of goods and services, approaching the breadth of the former GST regime. CIMB said broader exemptions for business inputs could reduce the cascading of tax costs through supply chains, although this would come at the cost of lower tax receipts. Veerinderjeet also does not expect an increase in the 2% dividend tax on annual dividend income above RM100,000, an extension of capital gains tax to listed shares or a further increase in the 30% top personal income tax rate in Budget 2027, according to the note. “Dr Veerinderjeet argues that the government should ‘sweat our assets’ through better collection, supported by greater investment in tax agency analytics. These efforts can deliver incremental gains, while broader personal, corporate and indirect tax bases offer scope to lift tax-to-GDP towards 15% over time,” said CIMB IB economists. Veerinderjeet estimates only 15% to 16% of the workforce currently pays personal income tax, with low wages limiting the number of taxpayers. Higher wages would therefore be important in expanding the personal income tax base. Budget 2027 is expected to be tabled in Parliament on Oct 9. The content is a snapshot from Publisher. title: 'Bursa Malaysia gains on Wall Street lead as weak US payrolls temper Fed rate hike expectations
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 5 — Bursa Malaysia opened higher on Monday, tracking Wall Street’s gains after softer US payroll growth eased expectations of an immediate Federal Reserve rate increase. At 9.10 am, the FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI (FBM KLCI) rose 5.01 points, or 0.31 per cent, to 1,635.88 from last Friday’s close of 1,630.87. The index opened 2.55 points higher at 1,633.42. On the broader market, gainers surpassed losers 224 to 158, with 337 counters unchanged, 2,054 untraded and 24 suspended. Turnover stood at 206.30 million shares worth RM98.78 million. Rakuten Trade Sdn Bhd vice-president of equity research Thong Pak Leng said the US 10-year yield remained elevated at 5.28 per cent and Brent crude oil settled at US$102.25 per barrel, keeping sentiment sensitive to interest rates and West Asia developments. “Over in Hong Kong, the Hang Seng Index slipped below 24,000 as financial and technology shares weakened. “Back home, following FBM KLCI’s higher close last Friday, we anticipate tentative stabilisation within 1,625-1,635 today, with bargain hunting offering some support amid a cautious market undertone,” he told Bernama. Among the heavyweights, Maybank, Public Bank, CIMB and Tenaga Nasional gained four sen each to RM10.06, RN4.70, RM7.69, and RM13.00, while IHH Healthcare decreased six sen to RM7.74. In active trade, VS Industry added three sen to 32 sen, Notion VTec increased four sen to 74.5 sen, GB Bond inched up half-a-sen to 23.5 sen, SFP Tech gained a sen to 28.5 sen, while Dagang NeXchange was flat at 51.5 sen. Among the top gainers, Samaiden put on 19 sen to RM3.03, UWC was 16 sen firmer at RM7.73, Critical Holdings perked up 15 sen to RM2.61, Mi Technovation strengthened nine sen to RM5.30, and Solarvest advanced eight sen to RM4.25. Nestle led the decliners, falling 32 sen to RM89.20, while Vitrox eased 14 sen to RM10.32, Kobay Technology was 12 sen lower at RM2.18, Kelington shed five sen to RM8.58, and YTL Power International edged down four sen to RM5.64. On the index board, the FBM Mid 70 Index gained 28.14 points to 17,510.07, the FBM Emas Index appreciated 33.81 points to 12,204.38, the FBM Top 100 Index widened 32.24 points to 11,989.92, the FBM Emas Shariah Index advanced 22.28 points to 12,082.60, and the FBM ACE Index improved 31.41 points to 5,560.87. Sector-wise, the Industrial Products and Services Index inched up 0.59 of-a-point to 179.11, the Energy Index gained 2.57 points to 835.60, the Financial Services Index jumped 97.59 points to 19,138.10, and the Plantation Index gained 2.23 points to 9,058.78. — Bernama

title: 'PTT Synergy beli 4 kilang dalam pembinaan bernilai RM32 juta di Klang jana hasil sewa berulang
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR 5 Okt — PTT Synergy Group Berhad bakal memperluas portfolio hartanah dengan pemerolehan empat unit kilang bernilai hampir RM32 juta di Klang, Selangor, yang disasarkan menjana pendapatan sewa berulang daripada penyewa industri. Menerusi makluman tambahan kepada Bursa Malaysia, ia berkata anak syarikat tidak langsung milik penuhnya, PTT Assets Sdn Bhd, akan memperoleh empat bidang tanah bersama unit kilang yang sedang atau akan dibina dengan jumlah pertimbangan tunai RM31.997 juta. Menurut kumpulan tersebut, pemerolehan itu bertujuan mengembangkan portfolio pelaburan hartanah kumpulan dan mewujudkan aliran pendapatan sewa berulang menerusi penyewaan keempat-empat unit kilang kepada penyewa industri. "PTT merancang memulakan proses mencari penyewa serta rundingan pajakan sepanjang tempoh pembinaan, dengan operasi sewaan disasarkan bermula selepas projek siap dan milikan kosong diserahkan, tertakluk kepada kerja pengubahsuaian yang diperlukan," katanya. Keempat-empat hartanah dijangka disiapkan dalam tempoh 36 bulan daripada tarikh perjanjian jual beli (SPA) masing-masing, dengan kerja pembinaan telah bermula pada 7 Januari 2026 dan kini mencapai sehingga peringkat rangka struktur bangunan, atau kira-kira 55% siap. Dari segi pembiayaan, risiko pembelian itu disokong kelulusan pinjaman daripada CIMB Bank Berhad dengan margin pembiayaan 90%, selain rebat Bumiputera 10% yang diberikan penjual. Berdasarkan terma pembayaran, 10% daripada harga pembelian perlu dibayar sebaik sahaja setiap SPA ditandatangani, manakala baki bayaran dibuat secara berperingkat mengikut kemajuan pembinaan sehingga notis milikan kosong dikeluarkan. "Pembelian itu turut mengambil kira transaksi hartanah perindustrian berdekatan, termasuk sebuah kilang berkembar di Bukit Raja Prime Industrial Park seluas 1,854.99 meter persegi yang didagangkan pada RM8.5 juta pada Jun 2026," jelas PTT. Satu lagi perbandingan ialah kilang berkembar di Bukit Raja 3 Industrial Park berkeluasan 2,024.99 meter persegi yang direkodkan pada harga RM7.689 juta pada Mac 2026. Sekiranya penjual gagal menyerahkan milikan kosong dalam tempoh 36 bulan daripada tarikh SPA, penjual perlu membayar ganti rugi dipersetujui pada kadar 5% setahun berdasarkan jumlah bayaran yang telah dibuat PTT sehingga tarikh penyerahan sebenar. Dari segi kedudukan kewangan, nisbah penggearan proforma PTT dijangka meningkat kepada 2.01 kali selepas pemerolehan berbanding 1.91 kali setakat 30 Jun 2025, berdasarkan kedudukan kewangan proforma yang dinyatakan syarikat. - DagangNews.com

title: 'This article first appeared in City & Country, The Edge Malaysia Weekly on September 28, 2026 - October 4, 2026
body: 'It was a scorching afternoon when Country Garden Pacificview Sdn Bhd (CGPV) executive director and chief of regional industrial business development Kevin Li and regional vice-president Syarul Izam Sarifudin arrived at The Edge ’s office in Petaling Jaya, Selangor. The pair had flown in from Johor Bahru to give an update on Forest City, a high-profile project in Johor that has dealt with some hot issues since its inception.  “What we achieved [since 2015] up to 2025 was merely concentrating more on our operational stability, resource integration and preparing for our next phase of growth,” says Syarul. “In the early years, we were primarily viewed as a residential real estate developer. But we are now embarking into a new sector — managing townships and driving actual economic nodes of financial and industrial development in southern Johor.”  The master developer of Forest City is a joint venture between China-headquartered developer Country Garden Holdings Co Ltd and Esplanade Danga 88 Sdn Bhd.  Operating as an independent local management unit under Country Garden Malaysia’s executive umbrella, CGPV is responsible for Forest City’s master plan development and management, industrial park development and Special Financial Zone (SFZ) operation.  Officially launched by the Malaysian government with duty-free island status in 2016, the 7,500-acre integrated development covers four reclaimed man-made islands over 5,000 acres and 2,500 acres on the mainland. Located in Iskandar Puteri, it sits along the Straits of Johor near the Malaysia-Singapore Second Link, just 2km across the water from Singapore.  The ambitious development has made international headlines over the years, some of them for the wrong reasons, especially since it has fallen short of market expectations in terms of progress, sales and occupancy rates. These challenges were compounded by the Covid-19 pandemic and the well-documented financial restructuring of its parent company amid China’s broader real estate liquidity crisis.  “When China’s property market faced a systemic downturn, amplified by global supply chain disruptions, macroeconomic shifts and strict pandemic controls, Country Garden — once China’s top property developer — was caught in the crossfire, just like many other big players in the country. However, late last year, our parent group successfully executed onshore and offshore debt restructurings in China,” says Li, who is also the chief financial officer of Country Garden Malaysia.  Regardless of the situation faced by its parent company, he highlights that Country Garden Malaysia operates with complete operational and financial independence.  “Since Country Garden entered Malaysia as its first overseas destination back in 2010 and 2011, the local operation has relied on an independent management team. For the past three years, our cash flow has been generated entirely within the country, allowing us to remain self-sustaining in terms of liquidity and debt servicing,” he says, adding that all five of its projects in the Klang Valley and Johor are performing steadily.  According to Li, Country Garden Malaysia’s sales and cash collection was RM1.3 billion in 2023, more than RM1.1 billion in 2024, and RM1.3 billion in 2025.  “More crucially, we utilised our local cash flows to fully settle bank borrowings and capital market obligations worth about RM2 billion over the past three years, including a RM1 billion sukuk … As at earlier this year, the remaining outstanding amount [of the sukuk] was only RM150 million. We pre-repaid them as our cash flow was comfortable.”  With most of its debts cleared, local rating agency RAM upgraded Country Garden Malaysia’s outlook rating from negative to stable in March, reflecting its balance-sheet resilience despite global sector volatility.  That financial stability has been supported by developments on the legal front. Malaysian courts have recently upheld the validity of sales and purchase agreements in favour of the developer. Dismissing buyer suits seeking to void contracts for reasons such as media portrayals of the project as a “ghost town”, the courts established that market downturns and post-purchase regret do not constitute grounds for breach. The decisions shield CGPV against speculative contract cancellations and protect its revenue base.  “Forest City has completed and delivered 26,000 residential units so far. We understand that we cannot make every single person happy, and it is normal to receive feedback or complaints. We respect the buyers’ legal rights,” Li says.  “But we also have our internal KPIs [key performance indicators] to meet. We are pleased to share that customer satisfaction consistently hits above 95% in our surveys and polls. Generally, the majority of our 20,000 residents are happy to live here, or they wouldn’t choose to continue staying. This is evidenced by our growing population.”  A city waking up  Today, Forest City is home to around 20,000 people living in 66 completed blocks, over 770 acres of the approved 5,000-acre reclaimed island land bank.  “If you pass by from Iskandar Puteri towards Batam, you can see the lights on across the residential towers at night,” Syarul says. “It is a night-and-day difference compared with what people experienced immediately after the pandemic in early 2021.”  Demographics have shifted significantly, he adds. While buyers were once predominantly mainland Chinese, the current resident base is largely local Malaysians, many of whom commute daily to Singapore or work in nearby industrial parks, as well as expatriates of different nationalities.  “The township’s commercial pulse is also quickening,” says Syarul. “The Fisherman’s Wharf commercial street has seen steady footfall, with duty-free shops, eateries and premier banking facilities, including branches of Maybank and CIMB, with Affin Bank and AmBank joining the fold soon.”  Forest City attracts between 1.5 million and two million tourists annually. Its crown jewel is Forest City Golf Resort, located on the mainland about 9km from the man-made islands. Featuring two 18-hole international championship courses, it draws golfers from Japan, South Korea and Singapore.  There is also an affordable beachfront water park that offers weekend entertainment for visiting families.  “Forest City is probably the only sandy beach in Johor Bahru. Otherwise, you have to go to Desaru, which is an hour away. To draw more visitors, we are also collaborating with some watersports academies on courses for adults and children. The beach and water park are very popular during school holidays and weekends, contributing to our growing annual tourist and visitor numbers,” Syarul says.  Meanwhile, Network School, a start-up society and experimental community based on Silicon Valley entrepreneur Balaji Srinivasan’s book The Network State, was set up in the township in October 2024.  Balaji’s private co-living and co-working hub at Marina Hotel drew hundreds of international digital nomads, crypto enthusiasts and tech workers.  However, in July 2026, the Iskandar Puteri City Council (MBIP) revoked the Network School operator’s business licence for breaching local licensing conditions. The management of the school clarified that CGPV operates solely as a commercial landlord, and that the developer is fully cooperating with the local authorities to ensure all commercial tenants adhere to the regulatory framework.  Strategic shift  Li says while Forest City’s master plan is unchanged, CGPV is shifting its focus towards commercial and industrial developments, in alignment with the government’s broader economic development plan for the state.  “We maintain the master plan as it is because, to us, it is still a very fantastic plan even after a decade. Of course, for such a mega development, you have to do it in phases, and there will be small twists and adjustments in between. But overall, we do not have plans to review the master plan. Now, we are embarking on the third phase of development. We foresee the entire master plan being completed only by 2040. It is now 12% to 13% developed,” says Syarul.  The biggest “twists and adjustments” to the master plan were its integration into the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ) and designation as an SFZ.  In August 2023, the government announced that Forest City would be designated as an SFZ to boost foreign investment, with incentives such as a 15% income tax rate for skilled workers and lower business operating costs. A year later, the government launched the tax incentive framework for the SFZ, which includes a zero tax rate for single family offices (SFO), a 5% corporate tax rate for fintech and global business services, and concessionary income tax rates.  In early 2025, Malaysia and Singapore signed a bilateral agreement to establish the JS-SEZ. Under the agreement, Forest City was formally incorporated as Flagship G, one of nine primary flagship zones within the 3,505 sq km economic zone.  “We started [the master plan] with residential and, maybe, this made people misunderstand that Forest City is focusing on high-rise residential developments. The SFZ designation puts us right back on track to [industrial projects],” says Li.  “Under the SFZ blueprint, the development is divided into two distinct functional zones, where the island component acts as a core financial services hub, focusing on single-family offices, fintech, foreign payment operating systems and back-office financial services. Meanwhile, the mainland focuses on smart logistics, high-tech manufacturing and global business services.”  To encourage direct investments in Forest City, the Malaysian government established the Iskandar Malaysia Facilitation Centre Johor (IMFC-J) at Forest City’s 42-storey primary office tower, Menara Delima Satu, to streamline the investment process. The centre houses 18 government agencies under one roof and acts as a single processing point for foreign investors.  “A key cornerstone of the SFZ is attracting family offices. The SC (Securities Commission) set an AUM (assets under management) threshold of RM30 million for family offices setting up in Forest City, a far more accessible entry point compared with Singapore’s S$15 million (RM47.9 million) requirement or Hong Kong’s HK$240 million (RM124.7 million) benchmark,” Li says.  Syarul stresses, however, that Malaysia is not competing with Singapore or Hong Kong in the SFO segment but is instead complementing them.  “It is about synergy. Under the SFZ rules, family offices in Forest City can invest up to 90% of their AUM globally. This means that investors can set up their operational base here in Forest City at one-third to one-fourth of the operational cost, while still leveraging Singapore’s capital markets just across the strait. It is very attractive to many family offices,” he explains.  Under the SFO Incentive Scheme guidelines issued by the SC, it is mandatory to establish a physical office in Forest City to qualify for and maintain SC approval and the accompanying 0% tax incentive.  According to Li, over 40 SFOs have secured physi­cal office space in Forest City, with nine having formally received SC approval to date.  “We are very positive about this, though we do not have an actual target of having many of them in Forest City in the near future because it is beyond our control and SC has its plan. But it is a strong catalyst in helping to add vibrancy to Forest City because when the offices come, they bring in their professional teams — accountants, lawyers and finance and investment experts,” he adds.  Forest City is also targeting global business services. CGPV is in advanced discussions with two major international banking institutions — one looking to relocate its back-office operations from Singapore, and another expanding its operational footprint from Kuala Lumpur.  Forest City 2.0  Despite the tailwinds from the SFZ, Li and Syarul acknowledge that transforming the mega project into a self-sustaining regional economy is not without immediate, real-world hurdles. The most pressing challenge currently is cross-border physical connectivity and accessibility.  “While the project is geographically proximate to Singapore, seamlessly moving people, goods and daily commuters across borders remains a complex, multi-jurisdictional effort,” says Li. “Furthermore, regional competition from peers like Thailand, Indonesia and Vietnam means that Malaysia must continually sharpen its execution speed and policy delivery to stay ahead.”  To close this connectivity gap, Country Garden is taking interim measures while lobbying government authorities for long-term infrastructure approvals.  “Before all the major government infrastructure projects are completed, we are bridging the gap ourselves. We currently run daily direct shuttles transferring residents and workers to the Sultan Abu Bakar CIQ Second Link complex,” Li says.  For the long term, the developer has submitted plans to the joint Malaysia-Singapore ministerial committee under the Iskandar Regional Development Authority (IRDA) for a dedicated ferry terminal. Once approved, ferry routes will connect Forest City directly to Raffles Marina in Singapore and Batam in Indonesia.  “We are also asking the government for assistance to permit a direct highway connection linking straight to Tuas, and to integrate Forest City into upcoming regional rail routes like the RTS [Rapid Transit System], ART [Automated Rapid Transit] and transport corridors heading to Kulai and Senai,” he adds. “Moving people efficiently is crucial to unlocking the full value of the JS-SEZ but because these are country-to-country matters, we have to keep pushing and following up continuously.”  Simultaneously, the master developer is pivoting to boosting population density and creating high-value local jobs, away from traditional residential property sales, towards what the team calls “Forest City 2.0”.  “We are not launching any more residential projects in the near future, but focusing on clearing the inventory. We will advance commercial and industrial land development earlier than originally scheduled to inject immediate economic vibrancy,” Li says. “Our next focus is to bring in companies and industries to invest or establish their presence here.”  Acknowledging the importance of generating sufficient jobs to increase Forest City’s population, CGPV is actively trying to draw data centres, logistics players and manufacturers to its upcoming 418-acre industrial park.  “We need to create real economic dynamics. If you don’t generate jobs and economic substance, you cannot sustain a population,” Li stresses.  The response to this industrial shift has been positive. In the first half of this year alone, the developer logged over 300 company enquiries and secured a 40-acre industrial land deal with a manufacturer in Phase 1 of the industrial park, paving the way for ready-built factory developments in Phase 2 should market demand sustain.  In another strategic partnership, Country Garden recently signed a term sheet with Penang-based Oriental Holdings Bhd (KL: ORIENT) to develop a RM750 million healthcare hub in Forest City, anchored by a 500-bed hospital alongside comprehensive medical supply chain services.  “Internationally, we are actively introducing Forest City to big-name [multinational corporations]. It is not so much for their name, but the entire supply chain. We are looking to bring in ‘queen bee’ investors,” Li says. “We have been doing roadshows, especially in China, to introduce the JS-SEZ and Forest City SFZ. We went to Shenzhen and Suzhou, which have some of the most successful industrial parks in China.”  Apart from the industrial park, CGPV has also received enquiries from international investors interested in private island parcels.  “It is something that we are looking at. Instead of standard residential towers, we can custom-reclaim approved island plots, such as 1.5 to two acres, based entirely on an investor’s specific operational or residential requirements. It’s about being adaptive to what the current market actually demands,” he says.  Road to 2030 and beyond  Apart from Forest City, Country Garden Malaysia has four other major developments in Johor and the Klang Valley, executed largely through JVs.  “Out of our five projects in Malaysia, four are structured as JVs,” Li explains. “Only Danga Bay is 100% held by Country Garden Malaysia. We welcome JVs because local partners bring value to the table, though for master site design, we prefer to lead.”  In Johor Bahru, Country Garden Central Park has completed three phases comprising over 3,000 residential units that are nearly fully sold. The developer is now planning subsequent sub-phases over a 10- to 12-year development cycle.  In Kuala Lumpur, the initial two phases of township development Lake City in Taman Wahyu are completed and sold out, with Phase 3 scheduled for launch next year. The remaining four parcels have been earmarked for development over a 15-year period.  In Semenyih, Selangor, residential development Diamond City launched its final landed parcel in September 2025, which is expected to wrap up construction within two years.  With a substantial land bank in its existing portfolio, the developer will focus its resources on executing its active pipeline over the next decade.  As the interview draws to a close, both Li and Syarul reflect on the long-term nature of master township development.  “Rome was not built in a day,” Li says. “When we first came to this coastal area in Johor, it was completely rural. Today, the infrastructure is firmly established. Development never moves in a straight upward line; it moves in spirals, but it always moves forward.  “We wish the public to know that since the first day Country Garden has been here in Malaysia, we have wanted to be here long term. Of course, there are twists and turns over the years, but we cannot deny the contribution of the company in Malaysia.”  He says Country Garden has invested RM32 billion in Malaysia, including RM20 billion in Forest City alone.  “We have created jobs, contributed to the country’s tax revenues and trained local skilled workers. Most importantly, after so many challenges and uncertainties, we were here, and we are still here today. The fundamentals are in place, and we have absolute faith in what Forest City will become.”

title: 'Monday wrap: Young architects rise, insurers rethink adequacy, AI trust gaps widen
body: 'Architecture's young talent, a shift in insurance strategy, AI trust gaps, and rising bank margins mark the week.  Last week in Singapore Business Review, eight architects under 40 were named for their work on hospitals, civic infrastructure, and heritage projects. Etiqa Insurance said the industry's challenge is shifting from expanding coverage to ensuring adequacy as customers plan for retirement and wealth transfer. Nearly all IT leaders reported artificial intelligence (AI) tools accessing sensitive data without permission, whilst AI shopping adoption climbed even as checkout trust lagged. Banks, meanwhile, are expected to see margins rise as SORA climbs toward 1.4% by year-end.  Singapore Business Review's list of notable architecture professionals under 40 for 2026 features eight honourees—five women and three men—from DP Architects, SAA Architects, RSP Architects Planners & Engineers, CPG Consultants, and Chang Architects. Their combined portfolio spans a $790m hotel (the largest Mercure property worldwide), Singapore's first fully integrated healthcare campus at Woodlands Hospital, and civic landmarks including One Punggol's Regional Library and the Goh Keng Swee Centre for Education, a 30-storey office tower under active construction.  Standout work included Kelvin Ng Si Hoa's role delivering Woodlands Hospital despite expressway noise and rocky terrain constraints, and Loh Zhu Ping's contributions to the $450m Funan Redevelopment and the $790m Mercure ICON Singapore City Centre.  Singapore insurers should shift focus from expanding coverage to ensuring policy adequacy, according to Etiqa Insurance Singapore CEO Claudia Soh, as customers increasingly treat insurance as part of long-term financial planning rather than pure protection against loss. Singapore's insurance penetration stood at 7.6% of GDP as of May 2026, ranking fourth among selected Asian markets behind South Korea, Taiwan, and Hong Kong.  A May CIMB report found 52.6% of residents viewed insurance as supporting financial independence, up from 45% in 2025, with customers increasingly looking at retirement, wealth-building, and inheritance planning. Soh said AI can help insurers tailor services but cautioned that "trust, human judgement, and meaningful customer relationships remain just as important."  Nearly all Singaporean IT leaders (98.9%) reported an AI tool or agent accessing sensitive data beyond its intended scope in the past year, the second-highest rate among eight markets surveyed in Delinea's 2026 Identity Security Report.  Despite 99.6% of organisations having a formal AI data access policy, only 14% of IT leaders can detect a scope violation as it happens, and 72% take a full day or longer to catch one—the highest globally. Employee behaviour compounds the risk: 84% of Singaporean employees said they have bypassed required approval processes for AI use, and just 38% of IT leaders said they can always trace a sensitive access event back to a named human authoriser.  Singapore consumers are increasingly shopping with AI, but remain wary of letting it complete purchases, according to Adyen's 2026 Singapore Retail Report. Whilst 72% of consumers use AI assistants for shopping, only 29% are comfortable letting AI complete a purchase, and 49% of existing AI shopping users hesitate at the payment stage.  Still, AI-referred visitors generate 53% more revenue per visit and convert 54% more than non-AI traffic. Separately, Salesforce's State of Commerce report found 82% of Singapore commerce leaders expect large language models to become essential to product discovery within the year, with agentic search usage as a shopping-journey starting point up 200% year-over-year.  Singapore's three-month benchmark borrowing rate is expected to climb to 1.4% by year-end, supporting bank margins into 2027, according to UOB Kay Hian. The three-month compounded SORA rose to 1.22% in the third quarter after falling to 1.02% in April, reflecting MAS's tighter monetary policy stance amid slowing money supply growth.  UOB Kay Hian raised its 2027 net profit forecasts for DBS and OCBC by 5.7% and 4.7% respectively, citing expected margin gains, whilst flagging risks from elevated US rates and potential Red Sea shipping disruptions that could push freight and oil costs higher.

body: 'Accelerating earnings and returns under Acceler8 This article first appeared in The Edge Malaysia Weekly on October 5, 2026 - October 11, 2026 Alliance Bank Malaysia Bhd Alliance Bank Malaysia Bhd (KL:ABMB) has made a clean sweep this year, bagging all three awards under the financial services (below RM10 billion market capitalisation) category. title: 'A record earnings run
body: 'This article first appeared in The Edge Malaysia Weekly on October 5, 2026 - October 11, 2026 CIMB Group Holdings Bhd Despite an increasingly challenging banking landscape, CIMB Group Holdings Bhd (KL:CIMB) has continued to set new earnings benchmarks, hitting a record net profit in 2024 before surpassing it with a fresh record in 2025. Net profit at the country’s second largest banking group and Asean’s fifth largest by assets rose 1.7% to RM7.86 billion in the financial year ended Dec 31, 2025 (FY2025), from RM7.73 billion a year earlier. That followed a 10.7% increase in FY2024 and a much sharper 28.3% jump in FY2023 to RM6.98 billion. The steady rise in earnings translated into a risk-weighted compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 19.6% over the three years — the highest among its peers. This made CIMB this year’s winner of The Edge Billion Ringgit Club (BRC) award for Highest growth in profit after tax over three years in the financial services sector, among banks that have a market capitalisation of at least RM10 billion. It also won in the BRC Super Big Cap category for companies with a market capitalisation of above RM40 billion. It is the third year running that CIMB has won in both categories, marking how far the group has come since the Covid-19 pandemic. Its return on equity (ROE) improved from 10.7% in 2023 to 11.2% in 2024 and 11.3% in 2025, from just 9% in 2022. Thanks to its strong share price appreciation and attractive dividends, CIMB also clinched this year’s award for highest returns to shareholders over three years in the Super Big Cap category for companies with a market cap of over RM40 billion. CIMB’s shareholder returns grew at a CAGR of 20.2% over the three years — ahead of the competition — as its share price shot up to RM7.55 on March 31, 2026, from RM4.35 on March 31, 2023. The returns reflect the higher dividends that shareholders received as profits grew. CIMB increased its dividend per share from 43 sen in 2023 to 47 sen in 2024, before declaring 47.1 sen for FY2025. Each year’s payout included a special dividend of seven sen per share. The latest payout amounted to a record of about RM5.1 billion. Supporting its share price is the fact that the group has committed to returning up to RM2 billion of additional capital to shareholders by 2027 through special dividends and/or share buybacks, subject to market conditions and regulatory approvals. This year, given a more challenging macroeconomic backdrop, including a prolonged conflict in the Middle East macroeconomics, CIMB’s 1HFY2026 financial performance softened from the previous corresponding period. Net profit for the period fell a marginal 0.2% year on year (y-o-y) to RM3.85 billion, while revenue slid to RM10.97 billion from RM11.10 billion. Be that as it may, it delivered an annualised ROE of 11%, in line with its target of 11% to 11.5% for the full year. It announced an all-cash first interim dividend of 19.65 sen per share, based on a consistent payout ratio of 55.5%, which translated into a total dividend payout of RM2.1 billion. Notably, asset quality remained broadly stable, with its gross impaired loan ratio at an all-time low of 1.6% at end-June, compared with 1.7% three months earlier. Group CEO Novan Amirudin said the execution momentum for Forward30 — the group’s six-year strategic programme that started running from last year — remained firmly on track. “Our destination is clear: to become the top-of-mind Asean bank by 2030. To get there, we must deliver a sustainable ROE of 12% to 13% by 2027 and compete consistently in the top quartile of our regional peers by 2030,” he said in the group’s latest annual report. Nevertheless, headwinds persist, and the group expects funding cost pressures in Indonesia and competition on loan repricing to weigh on its net interest margin (NIM) this year. CIMB’s NIM stood at 2.04% in 2QFY2026, down four basis points from the previous quarter and down 11bps on a y-o-y basis. A notable development this year is that CIMB’s Thai unit, CIMB Thai Bank, was delisted from the Stock Exchange of Thailand on Sept 12, more than 2½ years after a regulatory process triggered by stricter free-float requirements. CIMB Thai remains a core subsidiary and the delisting is not expected to have a material impact on the lender. The Thai unit is profitable, having posted more than a fivefold y-o-y increase in net profit to THB886.3 million in 2QFY2026. As at Aug 28, CIMB’s share price closed at RM7.96, giving the company a market value of RM86.05 billion. Bloomberg data shows 15 “buy” and five “hold” recommendations on the stock, with no “sell” calls. The 12-month average target price was RM8.88. “CIMB has balance sheet flexibility to navigate NIM pressure, and loan loss coverage buffers to weather any asset quality turbulence,” AmInvestment Bank Research said in a Sept 1 report. “The bank has also consistently proved itself as a strong strategy executor and good capital allocator. Besides, we like CIMB’s stance on returning excess capital, with scope for more beyond the planned RM2 billion programme, especially when its dividend payout ratio is about 10 percentage points below larger peers.” Save by subscribing to us for your print and/or digital copy. title: 'Share price soars as earnings continue to shine
body: 'Share price soars as earnings continue to shine This article first appeared in The Edge Malaysia Weekly on October 5, 2026 - October 11, 2026 AMMB Holdings Bhd Once again, AMMB Holdings Bhd (KL:AMBANK) is taking home The Edge Billion Ringgit Club (BRC) award for Highest returns to shareholders over three years under the financial services category. Notably, its share price has climbed steadily over the last five years, with the most significant jump recorded between 2024 and 2025. The stock gained 41.9% from RM3.70 on March 31, 2024 to RM5.25 on March 28, 2025. Between March 28, 2025 and March 31, 2026, the banking group’s share price continued its upward trajectory, reaching RM6.59, before hitting another record high of RM7.37 on Aug 12. Much of the enthusiasm about the stock can be linked to the potential return of excess capital to shareholders, which could either come in the form of higher dividends or through other capital return initiatives. AMMB, under its five-year strategic plan called “Winning Together 2029” (WT29), aims to double its dividend per share by the financial year ending March 31, 2029 (FY2029) from 22.6 sen in FY2024. This would be supported by earnings growth and capital optimisation, with Basel 3.1 reforms providing a meaningful upside catalyst. AMMB has already been increasing its dividend payout ratio, from 40% to 50% in FY2025, exceeding its earlier dividend payout ratio guidance of 35% to 40%. Total dividends increased from 22.6 sen in FY2024 to 30.2 sen in FY2025 and 35 sen in FY2026. Its three-year compound annual growth rate for shareholder returns totalled 27.9% for the period between March 31, 2023 and March 31, 2026. The increase in dividends can also be attributed to the yearly improvements in earnings. In FY2026, the group achieved its highest-ever net profit of RM2.1 billion, 5% higher than the previous year’s RM2 billion, driven by both net interest income and non-interest income. Net profit was RM1.87 billion in FY2024. Net interest income rose 4.5% in FY2026, backed by higher margins, while non-interest income grew 5.1% mainly from trading gains. For FY2026, the bank recorded a return on equity (ROE) of 10%, in line with its guidance to analysts. The group’s ROE has stayed at 10% over the last three financial years. In the recent 1QFY2027 financial performance, AMMB’s net profit came in at RM520.23 million, up slightly from RM516.18 million in the previous year on account of improvement in net interest income growth. The earnings were within analyst expectations. Non-interest income grew 5.1% year on year, supported by stronger wealth management fee income but net interest income was softer, compressing to 1.93% in 1QFY2027 from 1.97% in 4QFY2026, as competitive asset pricing and funding mix pressures weighed on margins. CIMB Securities has downgraded its call on AMMB to “hold” with an unchanged target price of RM7.35, based on 1.09 times price-to-book value (PBV). “While we remain constructive on AMMB’s medium-term capital return and efficiency story, we believe the key rerating catalysts from its recent WT29 capital management update are largely priced in. The next catalyst, the Basel 3.1-driven capital release, remains some distance away given its implementation date of Jan 1, 2028,” said the research house in a report dated Aug 19. It added that while further rerating under the FY2028 valuation framework is possible, the rerating will need to be supported by earnings delivery rather than valuation roll-forward alone. Meanwhile, HLIB Research — which has kept its “buy” call on the stock for a target price of RM7.80 based on an implied 2027 PBV of 1.1 times — said its loan growth should remain firm going forward, led by mid-corporate and wholesale banking, adding that it should start contributing more meaningfully to non-interest income from 2QFY2027. Nonetheless, it also warned that the prolonged Middle East disruptions could create further stress among selected Business Banking accounts, although the management is expecting around half of the current stage 2 exposures to revert to stage 1 by September if logistics disruption normalises. HLIB Research added that the capital appreciation still has legs, “propelled by the plausible rerating catalyst of a potential RM2 billion capital return from FY2028”. It has estimated that the capital return could translate into a dividend yield of over 8.5% for 2028. Save by subscribing to us for your print and/or digital copy.
