title: 'Inside the UN tunnel
body: 'Guillermo R Barreto In September, like every year, the UN General Assembly commences. Heads of state take the floor to send messages to the world. These messages are broadcast on TV, transcribed, and recorded in official documents and the press. We have heard denunciations of violations of international law, calls for peace and coexistence, and also cynical remarks from leaders of genocidal entities. It is a month of speeches that surely generates revenue for the media and benefits the local economy of New York City. It is month that also entails significant expenses for the delegations of the 193 UN member nations, in addition to the numerous NGO delegations present at or around the event. The UN was founded in 1945 following the end of the Great Anti-Fascist War, referred to as World War Two, by the Eurocentric narrative. Its purposes, principles and structure are set forth in the UN Charter, signed on 26 June 1945, in San Francisco and enforced since 24 October of that same year. As stated in Article 1, its purpose is to maintain international peace and security and to promote friendly relations among nations, based on respect for the principle of equal rights and the self-determination of peoples. - Sign up for Aliran's free daily email updates or weekly newsletters or both - Make a one-off donation to Persatuan Aliran Kesedaran Negara (ALIRAN), Maybank a/c 507246118995 or CIMB a/c 8004240948 - Make a regular pledge or periodic auto-donation to Aliran - Become an Aliran member Fundamental freedoms, respect for human rights, and universal peace – these are legitimate principles worth fighting for. The history of the UN, however, does not show that it has been capable of defending the principles for which it was created. Let’s look at three examples of this. In 1993 amid the war in the former Yugoslavia, the UN Security Council adopted resolution 819, which required the parties to the conflict (in this case, Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina) to treat the city of Srebrenica and its surrounding areas as safe areas, free from armed attacks or any other hostile acts. At that time, Bosnian Serb forces were carrying out an operation to displace and exterminate the Muslim population of Bosnia, thousands of whom sought refuge in Srebrenica, where they expected protection from the UN through its protection force Unprofor. This protection never materialised, and the Bosnian Serb army attacked, resulting in the massacre of 8,372 people. Even today, hundreds of bodies have not been located. Rwanda is another tragic case. There, the United Nations Assistance Mission (Unamir) was established to mediate the conflict that had been brewing and that led, in 1994, to the massacre of the Tutsi population by the Hutu army and militias. The reality is that, while the Security Council debated whether to use the term ‘genocide’ to describe what was happening, Unamir’s blue helmets were restricted in their actions, their personnel reduced to 250 troops, and the slaughter continued, leaving hundreds of thousands of people unprotected; they were ultimately murdered before the eyes of a world that watched without reacting. The words of the peacekeeping force commander, Romeo Dellaire, speak volumes: “I know that the mourning for all those Rwandans who placed their faith in us and believed that the UN Peacekeeping Force was there to stop the extermination, to stop the killings, and to guide them toward peace will never end. That mission, Unamir, failed.” Another UN failure is reflected in the United Nations Stabilisation Mission in Haiti (Minustah). A blue helmet intervention was launched to “maintain peace and security and support a political process leading to elections in 2010”. The mission remained in place until 2017, when its continued presence was deemed unsustainable. The conduct of Minustah soldiers has been heavily criticised, with numerous cases of rape and abuse of women and children. The introduction of a cholera epidemic (due to negligence in the management of wastewater from the blue helmets’ camps), caused some 9,792 deaths and affected about 820,000 people between 2010 and 2019. To date, the UN has not provided any form of compensation, and there has been no restorative justice for these cases. These are just three examples. The reality is that the UN was born with fundamental flaws: - A General Assembly where all parties have a voice and a vote and pass resolutions that are merely deliberative in nature and not legally binding - A Security Council composed of five permanent members with veto power and 10 non-permanent members – five of whom are elected each year for a two-year term – who, although they can make decisions, are severely limited by the veto power of the permanent members This is a self-perpetuating structure that, day by day, seems to be turning into an empty shell, powerless to transform an increasingly cruel reality. Twenty years ago, in an iconic speech before the UN General Assembly, the then-president of Venezuela, Hugo Chávez, said: “The United Nations system that emerged after World War Two has collapsed, shattered, it does not work anymore.” In that speech, Chávez called for the re-founding of the UN and put four proposals on the table: - The expansion of the Security Council in both the permanent and non-permanent categories - The implementation of effective methods for addressing and resolving conflicts - The immediate abolition of the veto power - The strengthening of the role and powers of the secretary-general Chávez added that it was necessary to move the organisation’s headquarters to another country that, unlike the US, would respect the host country’s norms by not imposing visa restrictions on delegations that are entitled to participate in the General Assembly and in the organisation’s own meetings and activities. For this year’s 2026 Assembly, the State Department is preventing the Palestinian delegation from attending. The General Assembly reminded the US government of its commitment to respect the host country agreement and voted in favour of Palestine’s participation. President Mahmoud Abbas will, however, have to participate via videoconference. Thus, we are currently witnessing increasingly aggressive and shameless actions by the US administration. This is an administration led by a narcissist surrounded by religious fanatics for whom international law holds no value and who act consistently to weaken the UN system and the principles of multilateralism. This is an administration that relies solely on military might to impose its will and uses unilateral coercive measures (neither contemplated nor endorsed by the UN) to force countries to submit to US influence. “The devil came here yesterday. Yesterday, the Devil was here in this very place. This rostrum still smells like sulphur.” This is how Hugo Chávez began his speech before the UN General Assembly exactly 20 years ago, on 20 September, one day after the speech by US President George W Bush – a phrase that echoed through the halls of the UN and made its way around the entire world. In that speech, Chávez unequivocally denounced the US’ ambitions to dominate the world, to install a ‘world dictatorship”, and to impose a “very original” democracy “through explosions, bombings, invasions and bombs”. Without hesitation, he labelled Bush a cynic for speaking to nations with hypocrisy while expressing his desire to control everything. Today, the US imposes its will even on its allies, wields a deadly military apparatus, and has no qualms about expressing its expansionist and controlling ambitions. The UN, on the other hand, appears to be an organisation incapable of curbing those ambitions or stopping the genocide of the Palestinian people, the massacres in Sudan, or the imperialist aggressions against Venezuela, Cuba or Iran. Can we expect anything from this 81st UN General Assembly? In his speech, Chávez spoke of the need to rebuild the UN. This need remains more relevant than ever. He also left room for hope by expressing reasons to be optimistic: “Streams, alternative thoughts and movements, youths with different ideas are rising.” That is where hope lies – in the capacity of organised peoples fighting for a different future – and not, for now, in the hallways and rostrums of the UN, where the air still reeks of sulphur. – Globetrotter Guillermo R Barreto is Venezuelan and holds a PhD in science from the University of Oxford). A retired professor at Simón Bolívar University in Venezuela, he served as the country’s deputy science and technology minister, president of the National Fund for Science and Technology, and ecosocialism and water minister. He is currently a researcher at the Tricontinental Institute for Social Research and a visiting scholar at the Center for the Study of Social Transformations-Ivic. title: 'AirAsia’s Hunt for Cheaper Debt Won’t be Easy With US$100 Oil
body: '(Sept 24): AirAsia Group Bhd’s (KL:AAGB) Tan Sri Tony Fernandes is fed up with private credit and the exorbitant interest rate they charge. “I don’t want to take any more private credit debt because it’s expensive,” the co-founder of one of the biggest Southeast Asian budget carriers said at a briefing last week. “I don’t want more debt. I don’t like debt.” While Fernandes is seeking to reduce interest payments — some as high as 11% — through a US$1 billion (RM4.09 billion) refinancing package, it may be tough for a company that sells cheap flight tickets to make money when oil prices are above US$100 a barrel. AirAsia’s finances are so strained that it loses money, has more liabilities than assets, and has a cash-to-revenue ratio that’s well below the industry standard. “AirAsia likely needs either a real improvement in operating cash flow or credit enhancement,” said Linus Benjamin Bauer, founder of aviation consultancy BAA & Partners. “Without that, cheaper money is difficult to justify.” Like most airlines, the Iran war hit AirAsia hard but the carrier, which doesn’t hedge its fuel costs, has been grappling with soaring prices to such extent that it went through two straight quarterly losses. Its total debt had surged to a record US$4.1 billion at the end of June, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. While the jump largely reflected Fernandes’ consolidation of all its airline businesses into AirAsia from sister firm Capital A Bhd (KL:CAPITALA), AirAsia’s liabilities exceeded assets by RM606 million as of end-June, according to the company’s first-half financial report. It also shows it had RM954 million in cash and RM18.4 billion in current liabilities due over the next 12 months, suggesting coverage of only 5%. The cash represents 4.3% of AirAsia’s annualized revenue of RM22 billion and “normal airline practice is to have cash and facilities of at least 10%-20% of annualized revenue”, said independent aviation analyst Andrew Light. Fernandes has received an offer for US$1 billion of financing from Middle East banks to refinance existing debt, but he’s holding off on a final sign-off while he searches for cheaper alternatives. AirAsia, which is also seeking RM700 million in local credit facilities, aims to complete the refinancing by December or January. AirAsia declined to comment on its recent fundraising efforts and whether talks with creditors reflected liquidity pressures or raised concerns about its ability to meet obligations without additional financing. “Unless Tony can present a credible business plan to get the airline back to positive cash flow, raising the money AirAsia needs on commercial terms will become increasingly difficult,” said Gerry Soejatman, an independent aviation analyst based in Jakarta. “That challenge will only get harder if oil prices stay elevated or rise further.” Highlighting its financial strain, AirAsia fell behind on dues to some suppliers and asked lessors to defer rental payments on more than 16 aircraft after fuel costs surged, Bloomberg reported in June. It had also asked private-credit lenders Ares Management Corp and Indies Capital Partners Pte Ltd to allow aircraft lessors to share revenue from routes pledged to their US$200 million facility. And since the start of 2025, it sold six brand new Airbus planes without ever putting them into service. Fernandes denied renegotiating with Ares, and said the jet sale reported by Bloomberg was inaccurate, adding the company was returning planes it didn’t need “in this crisis”. The planned US$1 billion in refinancing debt would save AirAsia around RM200 million a year in interest expense if it’s able to lower the interest rate on debt raised during the Covid pandemic and private credit to 7%-8% from around 11%, said Samuel Yin, associate director for equity markets research at Maybank Investment Bank. “The debt isn’t maturing this year, but the airline wants to prepare ahead of upcoming obligations. Given the rise in fuel prices, the costs are increasing,” said Yin, who said he met with AirAsia management earlier this month. Behind its fundraising efforts is a business that isn’t generating enough cash. AirAsia’s operations consumed RM582 million in the first half of 2026, according to its financial statement. Citigroup Inc downgraded its rating on AirAsia stock to sell from buy in a report this week, saying that its limited cash and equity buffers leave little room for another fuel-price shock. “We see jet fuel prices as the key determinant of future liquidity and profitability as balance sheet constraints remain,” Citigroup said. The Iran conflict has hit budget airlines particularly hard because they have less ability than full-service carriers to pass on higher fuel costs to passengers. The industry’s biggest casualty so far has been US low-cost carrier Spirit Aviation Holdings Inc, which collapsed in May amid soaring fuel prices and the failure of a government bailout. Fernandes has said his airline doesn’t need to be rescued by the Malaysian government, dismissing the idea of an intervention as “the most ludicrous statement I have seen in 25 years”. “AirAsia survived the pandemic without a government bailout and the brand has shown demand resilience,” said Bauer from BAA & Partners. “But with liquidity this tight, the margin for execution error remains limited.” Uploaded by Chng Shear Lane Source: TheEdge - 25 Sep 2026 Oct 01, 2026 Former Felda chief Faizoull Ahmad pleads not guilty to a 2014 cheating charge tied to 16 land plots and Synergy Promenade; court sets bail at RM70,000. title: 'Batu Kawan’s Takeover of MKH Crosses 95%
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR (Sept 30): Batu Kawan Bhd’s (KL:BKAWAN) unconditional mandatory takeover of MKH Bhd (KL:MKH) has crossed the 95% threshold, paving the way for the property developer’s delisting. As at market close on Wednesday, Batu Kawan and its wholly owned unit Whitmore Holdings Sdn Bhd, together with parties acting in concert, held 548.85 million MKH shares, representing a 95.16% stake, according to a statement issued on their behalf by Maybank Investment Bank Bhd. With the offeror having received valid acceptances of not less than nine-tenths in the nominal value of the offer shares, Batu Kawan and Whitmore will invoke Section 222(1) of the Capital Markets and Services Act 2007 to compulsorily acquire the remaining MKH shares from dissenting shareholders, the statement said. The takeover offer, it said, will remain open until Oct 8, following an extension from the original Sept 17 closing date. Bursa Malaysia Securities will suspend trading of MKH shares upon the expiry of five market days from Oct 8. Thereafter, Batu Kawan and Whitmore will procure MKH to take the necessary steps to withdraw its listing status from Bursa Malaysia. Two weeks ago, minority shareholders of MKH and its separately listed plantation arm, MKH Oil Palm (East Kalimantan) Bhd (KL:MKHOP), were given contrasting recommendations regarding Batu Kawan's dual takeover play. Kenanga Investment Bank Bhd, the independent adviser appointed by MKH, deemed the RM2 cash buyout “not fair but reasonable”, noting that the offer price undervalues the property developer’s fair asset worth. On the other hand, Mainstreet Advisers Sdn Bhd urged MKH Oil Palm shareholders to reject the related 66.26 sen per share buyout offer, labelling it "not fair and not reasonable". Mainstreet emphasised that the offer represents a steep 47% discount to MKH Oil Palm's net asset value, and noted that Batu Kawan intends to maintain the plantation unit's listing. The takeover was initiated in May, when Batu Kawan, through Whitmore, agreed to acquire a combined 47.7% stake in MKH from members of the Chen family for RM549.8 million, or RM2 per share. The RM2 offer valued the total cost of taking MKH private at up to RM1.15 billion, including the initial stake purchase. Batu Kawan's share price closed unchanged at RM20.52 on Wednesday, with a market capitalisation of RM8.2 billion. MKH also settled unchanged at RM1.99 with a market value of RM1.17 billion, while MKH Oil Palm closed unchanged at 64.5 sen, valuing the group at RM660 million. title: 'S P Setia Launches 100-acre Heritage Park at Setia Fontaines
body: 'S P Setia Bhd on Monday officially launched Setia Fontaines Heritage Park at Setia Fontaines, Kepala Batas, marking a significant milestone in the group’s continued placemaking and township development efforts in Penang. From left: Penang state executive councillor for tourism and creative economy Wong Hon Wai, Penang state secretary Datuk Dr Jafri Abdul Jalil, Yang di-Pertua Negeri of Penang Tun Ramli Ngah Talib, S P Setia president and CEO Datuk Zaini Yusoff and member of the Penang state legislative assembly Bukhori Ghazali. KUALA LUMPUR (Sept 21): S P Setia Bhd (KL:SPSETIA) officially launched Setia Fontaines Heritage Park at Setia Fontaines in Kepala Batas, Penang — marking a significant milestone in the group's placemaking and township development efforts in Penang. According to a press statement on Monday, the launch was graced by Yang di-Pertua Negeri of Penang Tun Ramli Ngah Talib and his wife Toh Puan Raja Noora Ashikin Raja Abdullah, alongside state representatives, government agencies, strategic partners, invited guests, residents and members of the public. Also present was Penang state executive councillor for tourism and creative economy Wong Hon Wai. "This effort not only enhances the value and appeal of Setia Fontaines as a premier township development but also contributes meaningfully to the broader socio-economic growth and development of Kepala Batas and the Northern Seberang Perai region," Wong said. He added that the project reflects the important role private-sector investment plays in creating sustainable communities, strengthening local economies and supporting the state's long-term development aspirations. Set within the wider Setia Fontaines development, the 100-acre Heritage Park incorporates a 63-acre man-made lake and a musical fountain to support quality living, recreation, wellness and community engagement. S P Setia president and CEO Datuk Zaini Yusoff said the launch reflects the group's long-term commitment to Penang and its belief that successful townships must be built around people, community and shared experiences. "Setia Fontaines Heritage Park represents our continued commitment to building beyond homes. Through thoughtful placemaking, green public spaces and community-led experiences, we are shaping Setia Fontaines into an integrated township that contributes to Penang’s growth while creating long-term value for residents, visitors and the wider community," Zaini said. He added that Heritage Park is envisioned as more than a township amenity, serving as a lifestyle and recreational attraction with potential to support visitation, public engagement and destination appeal for Seberang Perai Utara and the wider northern region. The official launch was followed by the Jom Mai Setia Fontaines Carnival, a large-scale community activation featuring family activities, Malaysia Day-themed programmes, cultural and entertainment performances, and tourism-related activations. Strategic collaborations with Tourism Malaysia, Penang Global Tourism and Maybank further supported the destination-branding direction of the programme. Setia Fontaines is planned as an integrated township in Kepala Batas, incorporating residential, commercial, recreational, lifestyle and future employment components within a single development. title: 'KLIA T2 Retail Occupancy Holds Steady Despite Airline Capacity Cuts
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR (Sept 29): Visitors walking through Kuala Lumpur International Airport's Terminal 2 (KLIA T2) will notice hoardings — temporary boards and barricades put up around shops that are empty or under renovation — at several areas of its retail section. While these appear just as airlines trim flight capacity to counter soaring fuel costs, the boarded-up spaces do not necessarily signal a broader downturn in the terminal's retail performance. Malaysia Airports Holdings Bhd (MAHB), which operates KLIA and 38 other airports in the country, said tenant occupancy at KLIA T2 remained resilient despite a decline in passenger traffic. Commercial occupancy stood at 93% currently, up from 92% a year earlier. “Some of the hoardings currently visible within the terminal are part of a planned reconfiguration of space to improve passenger processing and circulation,” MAHB said in an email response to questions from The Edge Malaysia. The airport operator said some commercial areas were being repurposed for this purpose, with several outlets in the affected areas scheduled to be progressively phased out by the end of the year. MAHB declined to disclose tenant level sales or passenger spending, citing commercial sensitivity. It said commercial performance depended on factors beyond passenger volumes, including passenger profiles, outlet locations, retail categories and the performance of individual businesses. The clarification comes as airlines operating from KLIA T2 contend with a sharp rise in fuel costs and weaker capacity on some routes since the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February. Global average jet fuel prices reached US$194.90 per barrel in the week ended Sept 18 — up 116.5% from a year earlier — according to data from Platts and S&P Global. Airlines have been particularly exposed to the increase because fuel typically accounts for between 30% and 50% of their operating costs. Budget carriers such as AirAsia Group Bhd (KL:AAGB) and Batik Air Malaysia, which remain largely unhedged, have been hit by the volatility in the jet fuel market. In response, some airlines have cut capacity by as much as 30% since April to limit fuel consumption and contain costs. AirAsia is the largest airline tenant at KLIA T2. Other carriers operating from the terminal include Scoot, Spring Airlines, Cebu Pacific Airways, Lucky Air, Qingdao Airlines and Shandong Airlines. On Sept 18, AirAsia said it had reduced capacity by 20% to 25% in the third quarter, traditionally a weaker travel period. It expects to restore capacity towards pre-Iran war levels in the fourth quarter, when year-end travel demand typically strengthens. The impact of the capacity cuts have been reflected in KLIA T2's footfall. While total passenger traffic across KLIA rose 2.1% year-on-year to 41.95 million between January and August this year, the headline growth masks a clear divergence between its two terminals. Traffic at Terminal 1 climbed roughly 8% y-o-y to 24.46 million passengers, but T2 saw numbers fall 5% y-o-y to 17.48 million over the same period. Still, MAHB said traffic had begun to recover from June. Total KLIA passenger movements increased from 4.7 million in June to five million in July and 5.2 million in August, with both terminals recording improvements. At T2, passenger numbers rose from 1.83 million in June to 1.86 million in July, and 1.98 million in August. “While T2 traffic remains below the corresponding period in 2025, the recent trend shows a gradual recovery following the capacity reductions experienced during the middle of the year,” MAHB said. The airport operator said it would continue to monitor airline capacity, passenger traffic and commercial performance. It added that the recent recovery in passenger movements provides a more balanced picture of conditions at both KLIA terminals than the weaker traffic figures recorded earlier in the year. For airlines, however, fuel remains a significant pressure point. In a Sept 21 report, Maybank Investment Bank Research estimated that every US$1 increase in the price of jet fuel could reduce AirAsia’s earnings by RM75 million. AirAsia shares closed half a sen or 0.94% lower at 52.5 sen on Monday, valuing the group at RM1.76 billion. The stock has fallen about 70% since the start of the year. title: 'Hap Seng Consolidated to Sell Singapore Listed Unit Hafary for S$140 Mil
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR (Sept 28): Hap Seng Consolidated Bhd (KL:HAPSENG) said it plans to sell its Singapore-listed building materials unit for about S$140 million (RM447 million) following a takeover offer. 23 Capital Pte Ltd is offering cash per share of S$0.64, or RM2.04, to take private Hafary Holdings Ltd and Hap Seng Consolidated has agreed to accept the offer for its 50.82% stake, according to an exchange filing. 23 Capital is a vehicle owned by the Hafary founding family. The proposed disposal will allow Hap Seng Consolidated to realise its investment in Hafary at a premium over its initial cost of just S$0.24 per share, as well as above market and historical trading prices, the company said. If the deal goes through, Hafary will cease to be a subsidiary of Hap Seng Consolidated, preventing any consolidation of any financial results. Hap Seng Consolidated will book an estimated gross gain on disposal of about RM187.3 million from the deal expected to be completed before the year ends. While it will miss out on future earnings from Hafary, “the proposed disposal enables the group to realise its investment in cash at an attractive valuation, thereby strengthening its financial position and enhancing financial flexibility”, Hap Seng Consolidated said. Proceeds from the sale have been earmarked by Hap Seng Consolidated for partial repayment of borrowings totalling RM6.9 billion at the end of 2025. Hafary, which manufactures and trades building materials such as tiles, stone, mosaic, wood-flooring, quartz tops and sanitary ware and fittings, contributed RM48.4 million to Hap Seng Consolidated’s profit and RM19.85 million in dividends. Low Kok Ann, a Singaporean and chief executive of Hafary, controls 23 Capital with his son Low See Ching and daughter Low Bee Lan. The elder Low, also known as Eric Low, started the business from a single ceramic tile shop in 1980. Hap Seng Consolidated bought into Hafary in 2015 as a stepping stone to expand in the region. At the time of the acquisition, Hap Seng Consolidated was mainly involved in upstream segment of the building materials market while Hafary was strong downstream. Maybank Investment Bank is as principal adviser to Hap Seng Consolidated while United Overseas Bank is advising the buyer 23 Capital. title: 'AHB Maintains Five Sen Income Distribution For FY2026
body: 'Amanah Hartanah Bumiputera (AHB) has maintained its income distribution at five sen per unit for the financial year ended Sept 30, 2026, benefiting more than 82,000 unit holders.  The final distribution for the six months ended Sept 30 was set at 2.1 sen per unit, alongside a 0.4 sen bonus distribution declared by fund sponsor Pelaburan Hartanah Bhd (PHB).  Together with the 2.5 sen interim distribution declared in April, the total distribution for FY2026 comes to five sen per unit.  PHB said RM120.13 million will be paid in the final round, bringing the total annual distribution to RM236.41 million.  The bonus distribution applies to the first 1,000,000 units held by each unit holder.  PHB Group Managing Director Mazuki Abdullah @ Muhammad said the full-year distribution reflected the resilience of AHB and its underlying property portfolio.  “AHB’s performance this year demonstrates our commitment to continue providing competitive returns to unit holders. At the same time, we remain focused on strengthening AHB’s position as an investment instrument of choice for Bumiputera investors through prudent capital management, dynamic investment strategies and continuous portfolio optimisation to ensure sustainable growth and long-term value creation,” he said.  PHB Asset Management Bhd (PHBAM) Chief Executive Officer Zulkifli Ishak said the fund manager would continue managing AHB responsibly to ensure it remained accessible to Bumiputera investors.  The distribution will be paid in the form of AHB units and credited directly into unit holders’ AHB accounts by Oct 13. The units will be automatically reinvested, allowing holders to increase their holdings.  Bumiputera investors can subscribe to AHB at a fixed price of RM1 per unit, with a minimum investment of RM100 and maximum of RM1 million. Subscriptions are available through authorised distributors including Maybank, AmBank, AmBank Islamic, Bank Islam Malaysia and Bank Kerjasama Rakyat Malaysia.

title: 'The Ladies 2026: 42 pemain mulakan saingan pusingan pertama - Portal Berita RTM
body: 'SERI KEMBANGAN, 1 Oktober – Pusingan pertama Kejohanan Golf Wanita The Ladies 2026 menyaksikan 42 pemain mula beraksi seawal pukul 7.30 pagi tadi. Saingan kali ini turut menampilkan gandingan pemain profesional serta amatur seperti Allycia Gan, Liyana Durisic, Durriyah Damian dan Kelly Tan. Menurut The Mines Resort & Golf Club, matlamat utama kejohanan tersebut adalah untuk melahirkan lebih ramai pemain berwibawa tempatan. Kejohanan tersebut juga sebagai batu loncatan penting sebelum saingan bertaraf antarabangsa menjelang kejohanan Maybank Championship tidak lama lagi. Penganjuran itu membawa mesej yang jelas kepada generasi muda bahawa kerjaya dalam bidang sukan golf profesional bukan mustahil untuk dicapai oleh wanita Malaysia. Kejohanan golf wanita, The Ladies 2026 rasmi membuka tirai menerusi acara Pro-Am Diraja di The Mines Resort and Golf Club, kelmarin. Kejohanan tersebut kembali buat kali kedua dengan menyasarkan visi menjadi antara kejohanan wanita berprestij di rantau ini, sebelum melangkah ke pentas antarabangsa. Kejohanan yang berlangsung di Kelab Golf The Mines dari 1 hingga 3 Oktober itu menawarkan jumlah hadiah wang tunai sehingga RM100,000.

title: 'Lelaki bebas tuduhan tipu RM108,500
body: 'Kota Kinabalu: Seorang lelaki bekerja sendiri berusia 50 tahun dilepas dan dibebaskan daripada pertuduhan menipu seorang lelaki membabitkan RM108,500 berkaitan beberapa projek di Kinabatangan dan Semporna. Majistret Wan Farrah Farriza Wan Ghazali memutuskan demikian selepas mendapati pihak pendakwaan gagal membuktikan kes prima facie terhadap Abdillah Hamzah. Abdillah dilepas dan dibebaskan tanpa dipanggil membela diri. Abdillah didakwa menipu Chong Kong Fah dengan memperdayakannya sehingga mempercayai bahawa tertuduh mengurus beberapa projek iaitu pembinaan jalan konkrit ke SMK Bukit Garam, Kinabatangan; menaik taraf sistem perparitan di Taman Perumahan Bukit Permata, Kinabatangan; membaiki jeti terapung di Dataran Lepa-Lepa, Semporna; menaik taraf jalan di kawasan Dolton Town, Semporna; dan membaiki rumah di Semporna. Pertuduhan menyatakan Chong memasukkan wang berkenaan ke dalam akaun syarikat bernama Dilwani Enterprise, yang tidak akan dilakukannya sekiranya tidak diperdayakan sedemikian. Kesalahan itu didakwa dilakukan antara 23 Jun 2016 dan 5 Disember 2018 di Maybank cawangan Semporna. Pertuduhan mengikut Seksyen 420 Kanun Keseksaan memperuntukkan hukuman penjara sehingga 10 tahun dan sebatan serta boleh didenda jika sabit kesalahan. Pihak pendakwaan memanggil enam saksi sepanjang perbicaraan. Timbalan Pendakwa Raya (TPR) Noor Hafizah Anggu hadir bagi pihak TPR Arfa Anchal Khan manakala peguam Nurul Rafeeqa Afdul Mutolip mewakili Abdillah. Sementara itu seorang lelaki berusia 64 tahun mengaku bersalah menyebabkan kecederaan parah terhadap seorang lelaki menggunakan parang. Bagaimanapun Hakim Mahkamah Sesyen Marlina Ibrahim menangguhkan hukuman terhadap Paul Akang ke 28 Oktober ini sementara menunggu laporan perubatan dan forensik. Sementara menunggu tarikh berkenaan, Paul direman lanjut. Paul didakwa menyebabkan kecederaan serius terhadap lelaki berusia 45 tahun itu menggunakan senjata berkenaan pada jam 5 petang, 21 September lalu di hadapan sebuah rumah di Kampung Kelansatan, Kuala Penyu. title: 'Mahkamah Tinggi kekal keputusan timbang tara anugerah RM77 juta kepada SUJV

title: 'Mahkamah Tinggi kekal keputusan timbang tara anugerah RM77 juta kepada SUJV
body: 'Kuala Lumpur: Mahkamah Tinggi mengekalkan keputusan Tribunal Timbang Tara menganugerahkan RM77 juta kepada kontraktor utama Menara Merdeka Maybank (sebelum ini dikenali Menara Merdeka 118). Keputusan tribunal menghendaki Global Wall (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd (GWM) membayar RM77,022,327.67 kepada Samsung C&T Corporation UEM Construction JV Sdn Bhd (SUJV) membabitkan pertikaian kerja fasad bagi projek mercu tanda berkenaan. Pesuruhjaya Kehakiman, Rajes Raghavuji menolak permohonan GWM mencabar keputusan itu, dengan memutuskan isu dibangkitkan sama ada secara individu atau kumulatif, gagal melepasi syarat bagi membolehkan keputusan tribunal diketepikan mengikut Akta Timbang Tara. GWM mencabar keputusan tribunal dengan alasan, antaranya melampaui bidang kuasa, pelanggaran keadilan semula jadi, kegagalan menimbangkan bukti dan hujah, tuntutan lanjutan masa dan kehilangan keuntungan. Rajes berkata, alasan itu secara intipatinya, adalah ketidaksepakatan terhadap dapatan fakta tribunal, keutamaan keterangan, dan tafsiran serta pemakaian undang-undang dan subkontrak oleh tribunal. Pertikaian timbul selepas GWM dilantik menjalankan kerja subkontrak fasad bagi pembangunan Merdeka 118. GWM menggantung kerja subkontrak pada 27 Oktober 2022, manakala SUJV kemudiannya menamatkan subkontrak berkenaan pada 18 Februari 2023. Perkara itu kemudiannya dirujuk kepada tribunal di hadapan tiga anggota terdiri daripada Ian Pennicott KC SC, Richard Wilmot-Smith KC dan David Bateson. Tribunal mendapati, kerja penggantungan kerja oleh GWM sah mengikut undang-undang, manakala penamatan subkontrak oleh SUJV adalah tidak sah. Bagaimanapun, selepas menentukan tuntutan dan tuntutan balas setiap pihak, tribunal memerintahkan GWM membayar RM77,022,327.67 kepada SUJV, faedah RM4,939,123.37 sehingga 16 Disember 2025, dengan faedah lanjut RM14,111.78 sehari dari 17 Disember 2025 sehingga pembayarannya diselesaikan. Anugerah kos berasingan memperuntukkan, 75 peratus daripada kos timbang tara memihak kepada SUJV. GWM menghujahkan, keputusan tidak munasabah kerana tribunal mendapati penamatan oleh SUJV tidak sah, namun masih memerintahkannya membayar lebih RM77 juta. Bagaimanapun, Rajes menolak hujahan itu, dengan menyatakan isu penamatan hanya satu daripada pelbagai isu dikemukakan di hadapan tribunal bagi penentuan. "Dapatan tribunal mengenai isu itu yang memihak kepada GWM tidak dengan sendirinya, menghalang SUJV daripada berjaya dalam isu bebas yang lain," katanya dalam alasan penghakiman diterbitkan Jabatan Kehakiman semalam. Rajes berkata, komponen tunggal terbesar dianugerahkan kepada SUJV ialah ganti rugi kelewatan RM33,561,503.39, yang timbul daripada kegagalan GWM menyiapkannya kerja mengikut tarikh siap yang dilanjutkan. Beliau turut mengambil perhatian, bahawa faedah RM9,691,621.22 timbul daripada pembalikan keputusan adjudikasi, manakala caj balik dan item pengambilalihan berpunca daripada dapatan ke atas tanggungjawab bagi kerja tertentu. Mahkamah juga menolak percubaan GWM untuk bersandar kepada kesan kumulatif aduannya. Rajes berkata, bilangan aduan tidak mengubah sifatnya yang, secara intipati, adalah cabaran terhadap merit keputusan tribunal. Beliau berkata, pihak-pihak sendiri memilih untuk membiarkan pertikaian mereka ditentukan panel tiga penimbang tara berpengalaman. Peguam Darshendev Singh dan Michelle Yap mewakili GWM, manakala Harold Tan, Serene Hiew dan Tan Joon Meng bertindak bagi pihak SUJV.

title: 'Tengku Ampuan Pahang rasmi Kejohanan Golf Wanita, The Ladies 2026
body: 'PETALING JAYA: Kejohanan golf wanita, The Ladies 2026 rasmi membuka tirai kelmarin menerusi acara Pro-Am Diraja yang dirasmikan oleh Tengku Ampuan Pahang, Tunku Azizah Aminah Maimunah Iskandariah Almarhum Sultan Iskandar Al-Haj di The Mines Resort and Golf Club. Kejohanan yang berlangsung selama tiga hari itu menyaksikan penyertaan seramai 50 pemain merangkumi kelompok profesional dan amatur termasuklah kemunculan semula juara bertahan, Liyana Durisic serta atlet Olimpik negara, Kelly Tan. Menurut The Mines Resort & Golf Club, matlamat utama kejohanan itu adalah untuk melahirkan lebih ramai pemain berwibawa tempatan selain bertindak sebagai batu loncatan penting sebelum saingan bertaraf antarabangsa menjelang kejohanan Maybank Championship tidak lama lagi. Katanya, penganjuran itu membawa mesej yang jelas kepada generasi muda bahawa kerjaya dalam bidang sukan golf profesional bukan mustahil untuk dicapai oleh wanita Malaysia. “Ia adalah satu jemputan kepada generasi baharu untuk melihat golf profesional bukan sekadar sesuatu yang dimainkan di tempat lain di dunia tetapi sebagai laluan kerjaya yang boleh diceburi oleh wanita Malaysia,” katanya dalam kenyataan. Dalam pada itu, saingan Pro-Am Diraja hari ini menyaksikan pasukan yang dibarisi Dianna Lee, Ang Bee Ee, Jojo Goh dan digandingkan bersama pemain profesional Kelly Tan dinobatkan sebagai juara keseluruhan. Tempat kedua diraih oleh pasukan Miran Shin, Raina Azene Ramli, Nur Azreen dan pemain profesional Tan Ying Ying manakala kedudukan ketiga disandang oleh Yang Amat Mulia Che Puan Besar Kedah, Che Puan Hajah Hamimah Haji Hamidun, Datuk Norfaizah Zainal, June Yap bersama pemain profesional, Zulaikah Nasser. Menurutnya lagi, selain memperkukuh pembangunan bakat tempatan, penganjuran edisi kali ini turut mendapat sokongan padu pelbagai syarikat korporat terkemuka seperti Prudential, 100PLUS, Power Root dan Delon. Jelasnya, pihak penganjur turut mempunyai perancangan jangka panjang untuk meningkatkan kualiti kejohanan itu dengan sasaran hadiah terkumpul mencecah kira-kira RM12.5 juta pada masa hadapan. “Objektifnya bukan sekadar meningkatkan wang kemenangan tetapi untuk mewujudkan acara yang mempunyai status kukuh bagi menarik perhatian antarabangsa, di samping memberikan pemain Malaysia platform yang lebih berkesan ke pentas global,” katanya. – UTUSAN

title: 'Amanah Hartanah Bumiputera maintains five sen per unit income distribution for year ended September
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 1): Amanah Hartanah Bumiputera (AHB) has maintained its income distribution at five sen per unit for the financial year ended Sept 30, 2026 (FY2026), benefitting over 82,000 unitholders. Pelaburan Hartanah Bhd (PHB), together with its fund manager, PHB Asset Management Bhd (PHBAM), said the final income distribution for the six months ended Sept 30, 2026, comprises 2.1 sen per unit, with an additional bonus distribution of 0.4 sen per unit declared by PHB as the fund's sponsor. "The bonus distribution will be applied to the first 1,000,000 units held by each unitholder. Including the interim income distribution of 2.5 sen per unit declared in April 2026, AHB’s total income distribution for the financial year ended FY2026 amounts to five sen per unit," the statement said. PHB said RM120.13 million will be distributed in the final round, bringing the total annual payout to RM236.41 million. PHB group managing director Mazuki Abdullah @ Muhammad said the full-year income distribution reflects AHB’s continued resilience and the strength of its underlying property portfolio, supported by PHB’s disciplined approach to asset and investment management. “AHB’s performance this year reaffirms our commitment to delivering competitive returns to our unitholders. At the same time, we remain focused on strengthening AHB as an investment avenue for Bumiputera investors through prudent capital management, active portfolio optimisation and strategic growth," he said. Meanwhile, PHBAM chief executive officer Zulkifli Ishak said the fund manager remains focused on managing AHB responsibly while ensuring the fund continues to serve as an accessible investment option for Bumiputera investors. PHB said income distribution will be paid in the form of AHB units, credited directly into unitholders' AHB accounts by Oct 13, 2026 and automatically reinvested, allowing unitholders to increase their unit holdings and potentially benefit from the long-term compounding effect. "Bumiputera investors who wish to subscribe to AHB may do so at a fixed price of RM1 per unit, with a minimum investment of RM100 and a maximum of RM1 million. "Subscriptions are available through the respective branches of authorised distributors nationwide, namely Malayan Banking Bhd (Maybank), AmBank Bhd, AmBank Islamic Bhd, Bank Islam Malaysia Bhd, and Bank Kerjasama Rakyat Malaysia Bhd," it said. title: 'Cover Story: How the AI tidal wave is reshaping the jobs market
body: 'This article first appeared in The Edge Malaysia Weekly on September 21, 2026 - September 27, 2026 FOR engineering outfit owner John, using artificial intelligence (AI) in his work has been a game changer. He “trains” the AI to write codes in the company’s style and now merely checks to ensure that the codes are written correctly. “I use AI to write more routine codes and it has helped me cut down coding time significantly, where a few days of work can be accomplished in 20 minutes. But I still need a few employees because engineers need to be at the physical location to make sure hardware is properly installed and conduct test runs,” he says. These days, the use of AI is prevalent in all aspects of life, in various sectors of the economy and professions, and more so among white-collar workers. Early research has shown that AI has, by some measure, improved the productivity of workers, but it still depends on the complexity of tasks and the user’s ability in AI prompting. Even so, AI is increasingly becoming part of everyday life. As a result, companies will soon be able to achieve the same outcomes with fewer workers — or, in some roles, none at all. The concern among white-collar workers about AI displacing jobs is real. Jobstreet’s Workplace Happiness Index found that while only around one-third of Malaysian workers feel “very” or “extremely” concerned about AI affecting their job security, the score is even higher among professional services workers, coming in at 47%. While there is no evidence of massive job loss as a result of AI at this juncture, recruitment agencies observe that job postings for certain roles have been declining. Jobstreet by SEEK in Malaysia managing director Nicholas Lam says AI is certainly putting pressure on some forms of white-collar work, particularly roles involving repetitive, standardised or administrative tasks, many of which are being automated. Current data points, however, more towards roles being redesigned than entire professions being replaced. “The clearest early signs of pressure are in selected content and administrative roles. Job ads for positions such as content writer, copywriter, secretary and graphic designer declined between 2024 and 1H2026. We see these trends as directional indicators that automation may be changing how these roles are structured, rather than proof of one-for-one job replacement,” Lam says. This observation is consistent with a May report by the International Labour Organization (ILO), which found that studies using job postings and online labour-platform data show a significant decline in demand for skills associated with routine writing and translation, following the diffusion of generative AI (GenAI) tools, alongside increased demand for AI-related skills such as machine learning and natural language processing. PwC Malaysia managing partner Soo Hoo Khoon Yean argues that the gradual redesign of work does not necessarily imply that workers will be displaced. Instead, he says, it points to a gradual shift in the mix of capabilities and skills required in those roles. “There may be a growing divide between workers who are able to integrate AI into their workflows and adapt to evolving skill requirements, and those who are unable to,” Soo Hoo says. “As AI becomes more capable, competitive advantage will increasingly come from areas where human strengths like context, judgement and accountability matter most. This includes making high-stakes decisions, solving nuanced problems, managing stakeholder relationships, and bringing together insights from different disciplines to create solutions that AI alone cannot deliver.” Such expectations are starting to show up in the hiring landscape in Malaysia, with AI or digital tools becoming more common in the workplace. Randstad Malaysia associate director, emerging technology recruitment Dylan Long sees a clear shift in Malaysia’s hiring landscape, where employers are increasingly prioritising talent who are adept in AI and digital tools. “This trend is no longer confined to specialised tech departments; instead, having basic knowledge and practical experience with AI has rapidly evolved into a fundamental, baseline requirement for almost any professional role. There is an immense demand for individuals who demonstrate high digital agility,” Long says. He adds that a proactive willingness to embrace self-directed learning and integrate AI into one’s routine work has become a powerful, highly attractive differentiator in the current market. Statistics from Jobstreet confirm this change in the hiring landscape. According to Lam, the recruitment agency’s data shows that 70% of employers factor AI knowledge into hiring decisions, while one in three treat AI capability as a core hiring requirement. At the same time, demand for dedicated AI hiring is also increasing rapidly, notes Lam. AI-labelled job ads grew by 131% year on year in 2025. In 1H2026, the number of AI-labelled job ads was already 24% higher than the total for the whole of 2025, he says. One question that has often been raised is whether junior hiring will be reduced as a result of AI proliferation. A Gartner Inc survey carried out late last year found that 22% of chief human resources officers in the US reported that at least one business leader in their organisation has stopped hiring for entry-level roles as a result of AI automation. Some argue that removing the routine or repetitive tasks traditionally assigned to junior staff — often a training ground for developing judgement and gaining crucial experience — could ultimately hurt organisations by weakening their future talent pipeline. According to Soo Hoo, however, PwC’s global research shows that the bar is now higher for junior talent, with emotional quotient, judgement and leadership skills — qualities normally expected of senior hires — being prioritised. “Organisations will need to rethink how early-career talent is developed, including creating new pathways through which early-career employees can learn through application and experience,” he says. “Traditional apprenticeship models built largely around repetitive tasks may need to evolve into more structured experiences that accelerate the development of these broader capabilities.” Sufficient AI talent in Malaysia? While employers today want workers who can use AI in ways that help create value, there is also a need for AI developer roles in the country, notes Soo Hoo. “Malaysia needs to strengthen both the depth and breadth of its AI talent base. Findings from our 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer indicate that AI-related roles in Malaysia are currently concentrated in roles that apply AI in business functions (AI user roles) rather than roles focused on developing core AI technologies (AI developer roles),” he says. Soo Hoo cautions that the pipeline of specialised AI talent in Malaysia may not be sustainable for the country’s long-term ambitions, given the pace at which AI is evolving. “Malaysia needs both AI user and AI developer roles in our journey towards realising our AI Nation 2030 aspirations. We need to expand the pool of highly specialised engineers, data scientists and technical experts who can develop and commercialise homegrown digital innovation. At the same time, we must equip workers across sectors with AI literacy, applied skills and judgement to use these technologies productively and responsibly,” he explains. Having said that, every paradigm change will have its drawbacks. Human resources practitioners are reporting that, because of the speed at which the AI world is moving, employees are starting to experience AI fatigue, or “AI brain fry”, as they try to keep pace with the changes. “Companies need to think about the pace at which and direction in which they are adopting AI in their systems and processes. AI fatigue is a real issue and it’s not because employees are not eager to learn. This could result in a decrease, instead of an increase, in efficiency and productivity,” says an HR practitioner. A human resources director with a local company says some employees might not want to go down the AI rabbit hole. “We have reskilling programmes where we reassign certain affected roles to other areas in the company. But some of our employees, typically those who are closer to retirement, say they would rather opt for an early retirement plan, instead of reskilling,” notes the director. State of the labour market Minister of Economic Affairs Akmal Nasrullah Mohd Nasir said last Friday that a total of 68,177 workers lost their jobs from January to Sept 16, representing an increase of 15,196 over the same period last year. A recent report on the Social Security Organisation’s Employment Insurance Scheme (EIS) shows that professionals, managers, executives and technicians was the occupation category that saw the highest retrenchment rate, at 51% of the total loss of employment (LOE) benefit applications. It is not a new phenomenon, however, and has been in line with the data from 2021 to 2025. While some have attributed the higher retrenchment numbers partly to the increased adoption of AI or automation in companies, Maybank Investment Bank group chief economist Suhaimi Illias says it is still too early to determine the extent to which AI is driving retrenchments. He points out that Malaysia’s level of AI adoption, compared to other countries around the world, is still moderate. Citing the Microsoft AI Economy Institute’s Global AI Diffusion Scoring, he highlights that Malaysia ranked 51 out of 147 countries, with AI users accounting for 21.8% of the working-age population as at 1Q2026. Countries ranked among the top 20 have AI adoption rates ranging from more than 30% to 70%. “There are also other factors behind the higher share of skilled-worker retrenchments. Voluntary/Mutual Separation Schemes or Early Retirement Planning (VSS/MSS/ERP) have consistently ranked among the top three reasons for retrenchments and were the leading reason between 2023 and 2025. Higher-skilled employees may be more inclined to participate in such schemes, given attractive payouts,” Suhaimi says. He adds that the spike in total retrenchments may also reflect companies managing rising cost pressures through headcount reductions. This year, while the Consumer Price Index has remained moderate at 1.9% y-o-y in June, from 1.4% in February, the Producer Price Index has seen a spike to 9.2% y-o-y, from -3.4%, implying that companies have not passed down much of their higher cost to consumers so far. Interestingly, the country’s unemployment rate has held steady around 3% despite rising retrenchments. Suhaimi explains that because job placements continue to outpace layoffs, the economy is still net-positive for job creation. In 1H2026, placements reached 74,874, significantly higher than the 47,030 retrenchments. The way forward for employees With 620,000 jobs in Malaysia expected to be reshaped by AI, digitalisation and the green economy over the next three to five years, Jobstreet’s Lam warns that early-career professionals must learn to use these technologies both practically and responsibly. “AI literacy should increasingly be treated as a baseline capability,” he adds. Still, being literate in digital tools alone is not enough. Randstad’s Long points out the younger generation are naturally adept at using and eager to adopt new technology, but global employers still prefer “job-ready” candidates who have practical experience. “New graduates can prepare by actively seeking out structured internships, graduate trainee programmes, and on-the-job training opportunities that offer direct exposure to complex, real-world projects,” he says. “In fact, according to the Randstad 2026 Job Market Outlook and Salary Guide report, continuous learning has become such a non-negotiable for long-term career security that 56% of Gen Z talent in Malaysia would outright reject a job offer if it did not provide clear learning and development pathways to future-proof their skills.” Meanwhile, Long notes that mid- to late-career professionals must future-proof themselves by blending their vast experience with modern technological efficiency. title: 'Cover Story: How the AI tidal wave is reshaping the jobs market
body: 'Cover Story: How the AI tidal wave is reshaping the jobs market This article first appeared in The Edge Malaysia Weekly on September 21, 2026 - September 27, 2026 FOR engineering outfit owner John, using artificial intelligence (AI) in his work has been a game changer. He “trains” the AI to write codes in the company’s style and now merely checks to ensure that the codes are written correctly. “I use AI to write more routine codes and it has helped me cut down coding time significantly, where a few days of work can be accomplished in 20 minutes. But I still need a few employees because engineers need to be at the physical location to make sure hardware is properly installed and conduct test runs,” he says. These days, the use of AI is prevalent in all aspects of life, in various sectors of the economy and professions, and more so among white-collar workers. Early research has shown that AI has, by some measure, improved the productivity of workers, but it still depends on the complexity of tasks and the user’s ability in AI prompting. Even so, AI is increasingly becoming part of everyday life. As a result, companies will soon be able to achieve the same outcomes with fewer workers — or, in some roles, none at all. The concern among white-collar workers about AI displacing jobs is real. Jobstreet’s Workplace Happiness Index found that while only around one-third of Malaysian workers feel “very” or “extremely” concerned about AI affecting their job security, the score is even higher among professional services workers, coming in at 47%. While there is no evidence of massive job loss as a result of AI at this juncture, recruitment agencies observe that job postings for certain roles have been declining. Jobstreet by SEEK in Malaysia managing director Nicholas Lam says AI is certainly putting pressure on some forms of white-collar work, particularly roles involving repetitive, standardised or administrative tasks, many of which are being automated. Current data points, however, more towards roles being redesigned than entire professions being replaced. “The clearest early signs of pressure are in selected content and administrative roles. Job ads for positions such as content writer, copywriter, secretary and graphic designer declined between 2024 and 1H2026. We see these trends as directional indicators that automation may be changing how these roles are structured, rather than proof of one-for-one job replacement,” Lam says. This observation is consistent with a May report by the International Labour Organization (ILO), which found that studies using job postings and online labour-platform data show a significant decline in demand for skills associated with routine writing and translation, following the diffusion of generative AI (GenAI) tools, alongside increased demand for AI-related skills such as machine learning and natural language processing. PwC Malaysia managing partner Soo Hoo Khoon Yean argues that the gradual redesign of work does not necessarily imply that workers will be displaced. Instead, he says, it points to a gradual shift in the mix of capabilities and skills required in those roles. “There may be a growing divide between workers who are able to integrate AI into their workflows and adapt to evolving skill requirements, and those who are unable to,” Soo Hoo says. “As AI becomes more capable, competitive advantage will increasingly come from areas where human strengths like context, judgement and accountability matter most. This includes making high-stakes decisions, solving nuanced problems, managing stakeholder relationships, and bringing together insights from different disciplines to create solutions that AI alone cannot deliver.” Such expectations are starting to show up in the hiring landscape in Malaysia, with AI or digital tools becoming more common in the workplace. Randstad Malaysia associate director, emerging technology recruitment Dylan Long sees a clear shift in Malaysia’s hiring landscape, where employers are increasingly prioritising talent who are adept in AI and digital tools. “This trend is no longer confined to specialised tech departments; instead, having basic knowledge and practical experience with AI has rapidly evolved into a fundamental, baseline requirement for almost any professional role. There is an immense demand for individuals who demonstrate high digital agility,” Long says. He adds that a proactive willingness to embrace self-directed learning and integrate AI into one’s routine work has become a powerful, highly attractive differentiator in the current market. Statistics from Jobstreet confirm this change in the hiring landscape. According to Lam, the recruitment agency’s data shows that 70% of employers factor AI knowledge into hiring decisions, while one in three treat AI capability as a core hiring requirement. At the same time, demand for dedicated AI hiring is also increasing rapidly, notes Lam. AI-labelled job ads grew by 131% year on year in 2025. In 1H2026, the number of AI-labelled job ads was already 24% higher than the total for the whole of 2025, he says. One question that has often been raised is whether junior hiring will be reduced as a result of AI proliferation. A Gartner Inc survey carried out late last year found that 22% of chief human resources officers in the US reported that at least one business leader in their organisation has stopped hiring for entry-level roles as a result of AI automation. Some argue that removing the routine or repetitive tasks traditionally assigned to junior staff — often a training ground for developing judgement and gaining crucial experience — could ultimately hurt organisations by weakening their future talent pipeline. According to Soo Hoo, however, PwC’s global research shows that the bar is now higher for junior talent, with emotional quotient, judgement and leadership skills — qualities normally expected of senior hires — being prioritised. “Organisations will need to rethink how early-career talent is developed, including creating new pathways through which early-career employees can learn through application and experience,” he says. “Traditional apprenticeship models built largely around repetitive tasks may need to evolve into more structured experiences that accelerate the development of these broader capabilities.” Sufficient AI talent in Malaysia? While employers today want workers who can use AI in ways that help create value, there is also a need for AI developer roles in the country, notes Soo Hoo. “Malaysia needs to strengthen both the depth and breadth of its AI talent base. Findings from our 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer indicate that AI-related roles in Malaysia are currently concentrated in roles that apply AI in business functions (AI user roles) rather than roles focused on developing core AI technologies (AI developer roles),” he says. Soo Hoo cautions that the pipeline of specialised AI talent in Malaysia may not be sustainable for the country’s long-term ambitions, given the pace at which AI is evolving. “Malaysia needs both AI user and AI developer roles in our journey towards realising our AI Nation 2030 aspirations. We need to expand the pool of highly specialised engineers, data scientists and technical experts who can develop and commercialise homegrown digital innovation. At the same time, we must equip workers across sectors with AI literacy, applied skills and judgement to use these technologies productively and responsibly,” he explains. Having said that, every paradigm change will have its drawbacks. Human resources practitioners are reporting that, because of the speed at which the AI world is moving, employees are starting to experience AI fatigue, or “AI brain fry”, as they try to keep pace with the changes. “Companies need to think about the pace at which and direction in which they are adopting AI in their systems and processes. AI fatigue is a real issue and it’s not because employees are not eager to learn. This could result in a decrease, instead of an increase, in efficiency and productivity,” says an HR practitioner. A human resources director with a local company says some employees might not want to go down the AI rabbit hole. “We have reskilling programmes where we reassign certain affected roles to other areas in the company. But some of our employees, typically those who are closer to retirement, say they would rather opt for an early retirement plan, instead of reskilling,” notes the director. State of the labour market Minister of Economic Affairs Akmal Nasrullah Mohd Nasir said last Friday that a total of 68,177 workers lost their jobs from January to Sept 16, representing an increase of 15,196 over the same period last year. A recent report on the Social Security Organisation’s Employment Insurance Scheme (EIS) shows that professionals, managers, executives and technicians was the occupation category that saw the highest retrenchment rate, at 51% of the total loss of employment (LOE) benefit applications. It is not a new phenomenon, however, and has been in line with the data from 2021 to 2025. While some have attributed the higher retrenchment numbers partly to the increased adoption of AI or automation in companies, Maybank Investment Bank group chief economist Suhaimi Illias says it is still too early to determine the extent to which AI is driving retrenchments. He points out that Malaysia’s level of AI adoption, compared to other countries around the world, is still moderate. Citing the Microsoft AI Economy Institute’s Global AI Diffusion Scoring, he highlights that Malaysia ranked 51 out of 147 countries, with AI users accounting for 21.8% of the working-age population as at 1Q2026. Countries ranked among the top 20 have AI adoption rates ranging from more than 30% to 70%. “There are also other factors behind the higher share of skilled-worker retrenchments. Voluntary/Mutual Separation Schemes or Early Retirement Planning (VSS/MSS/ERP) have consistently ranked among the top three reasons for retrenchments and were the leading reason between 2023 and 2025. Higher-skilled employees may be more inclined to participate in such schemes, given attractive payouts,” Suhaimi says. He adds that the spike in total retrenchments may also reflect companies managing rising cost pressures through headcount reductions. This year, while the Consumer Price Index has remained moderate at 1.9% y-o-y in June, from 1.4% in February, the Producer Price Index has seen a spike to 9.2% y-o-y, from -3.4%, implying that companies have not passed down much of their higher cost to consumers so far. Interestingly, the country’s unemployment rate has held steady around 3% despite rising retrenchments. Suhaimi explains that because job placements continue to outpace layoffs, the economy is still net-positive for job creation. In 1H2026, placements reached 74,874, significantly higher than the 47,030 retrenchments. The way forward for employees With 620,000 jobs in Malaysia expected to be reshaped by AI, digitalisation and the green economy over the next three to five years, Jobstreet’s Lam warns that early-career professionals must learn to use these technologies both practically and responsibly. “AI literacy should increasingly be treated as a baseline capability,” he adds. Still, being literate in digital tools alone is not enough. Randstad’s Long points out the younger generation are naturally adept at using and eager to adopt new technology, but global employers still prefer “job-ready” candidates who have practical experience. “New graduates can prepare by actively seeking out structured internships, graduate trainee programmes, and on-the-job training opportunities that offer direct exposure to complex, real-world projects,” he says. “In fact, according to the Randstad 2026 Job Market Outlook and Salary Guide report, continuous learning has become such a non-negotiable for long-term career security that 56% of Gen Z talent in Malaysia would outright reject a job offer if it did not provide clear learning and development pathways to future-proof their skills.” Meanwhile, Long notes that mid- to late-career professionals must future-proof themselves by blending their vast experience with modern technological efficiency. Ultimately, Lam concludes, today’s workforce — regardless of seniority — should strive to work with AI while sharpening the human and commercial skills that technology cannot easily replicate. title: 'Man freed of RM108,500 cheating charge
body: 'Kota Kinabalu: A 50-year-old self-employed was freed from a charge of cheating a man involving a sum of RM108,500 over several projects in Kinabatangan and Semporna. Magistrate Wan Farrah Farriza Wan Ghazali discharged and acquitted Abdillah Hamzah without his defence being called after ruling that the prosecution had failed to establish a prima facie case against him. Abdillah was accused of cheating one Chong Kong Fah by deceiving him into believing that Abdillah had managed the following projects namely, to build a concrete road to SMK Bukit Garam, Kinabatangan, to upgrade the drainage system at Bukit Permata Housing Estate, Kinabatangan, to repair the floating Jetty at Dataran Lepa-Lepa, Semporna, to upgrade the road in the Dolton Town area, Semporna and to repair houses in Semporna. The charge stated that Chong had banked-in the money into a company account under the name of Dilwani Enterprise, which he would not have done had he not been so deceived. The offence allegedly took place between June 23, 2016 and Dec 5, 2018 at the Maybank in Semporna branch. The offence under Section 420 of the Penal Code carries a jail term of up to 10 years and whipping, and liable to a fine, on conviction. The prosecution had called six witnesses during the hearing. Deputy Public Prosecutor (DPP) Noor Hafizah Anggu standing in for DPP Arfa Anchal Khan while counsel Nurul Rafeeqa Afdul Mutolip defended Abdillah. Meanwhile, a 64-year-old man pleaded guilty to causing grievous injury to another man with a machete. However, Sessions Court Judge Marlina Ibrahim deferred Paul Akang’s sentencing to Oct 28 this year pending medical and forensic reports. Pending the date, Paul was further remanded. Paul is accused of causing serious injury to the 45-year-old man by using the weapon at 5pm on Sept 21 this year in front of a house in Kg Kelansatan, Kuala Penyu. DPP Ronnie Antony prosecuted the case. Man freed of RM108,500 cheating charge Daily Express Daily Express Online (Malaysia) is Sabah's top-ranked & most viewed English news site. title: 'AHB kekalkan agihan pendapatan lima sen seunit bagi tahun kewangan 2026
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR: Amanah Hartanah Bumiputera (AHB) mengekalkan agihan pendapatan sebanyak lima sen seunit bagi tahun kewangan berakhir 30 Sept 2026, yang memberi manfaat kepada lebih 82,000 pemegang unit. Pelaburan Hartanah Bhd (PHB) bersama pengurus dananya, PHB Asset Management Bhd (PHBAM), berkata agihan pendapatan akhir bagi tempoh enam bulan berakhir 30 Sept 2026 adalah sebanyak 2.1 sen seunit, dengan tambahan agihan bonus sebanyak 0.4 sen seunit yang diisytiharkan PHB selaku penaja dana itu. “Edaran bonus itu akan diberikan bagi 1,000,000 unit pertama bagi setiap pemegang unit. Dengan mengambil kira agihan pendapatan interim sebanyak 2.5 sen seunit yang diisytiharkan pada April 2026, jumlah keseluruhan agihan pendapatan AHB bagi tahun kewangan berakhir 2026 adalah lima sen seunit,” menurut kenyataan itu. PHB berkata sebanyak RM120.13 juta akan diagihkan pada pusingan akhir, menjadikan jumlah keseluruhan agihan tahunan sebanyak RM236.41 juta. Pengarah Urusan kumpulan PHB Mazuki Abdullah @ Muhammad berkata agihan pendapatan bagi setahun penuh itu mencerminkan daya tahan AHB yang berterusan serta kekuatan portfolio hartanah asasnya, disokong pendekatan pengurusan aset dan pelaburan yang berdisiplin oleh PHB. “Prestasi AHB tahun ini membuktikan komitmen kami untuk terus memberikan pulangan yang kompetitif kepada pemegang unit. “Pada masa sama, kami kekal memberi tumpuan kepada usaha memperkukuh kedudukan AHB sebagai instrumen pelaburan pilihan pelabur Bumiputera menerusi pengurusan modal yang berhemat, strategi pelaburan yang dinamik serta pengoptimuman portfolio yang berterusan bagi memastikan pertumbuhan yang mampan danpenciptaan nilai jangka panjang,” katanya. Sementara itu, Ketua Pegawai Eksekutif PHBAM Zulkifli Ishak berkata pengurus dana itu kekal fokus menguruskan AHB secara bertanggungjawab bagi memastikan dana berkenaan terus menjadi pilihan pelaburan yang mudah diakses oleh pelabur Bumiputera. PHB berkata agihan pendapatan itu akan dibayar dalam bentuk unit AHB yang dikreditkan terus ke dalam akaun AHB pemegang unit selewat-lewatnya pada 13 Okt 2026. Agihan tersebut akan dilaburkan semula secara automatik, sekali gus membolehkan pemegang unit menambah pegangan unit serta berpotensi menikmati kesan pengkompaunan dalam jangka panjang. “Pelabur Bumiputera yang ingin melanggan AHB boleh berbuat demikian pada harga tetap RM1 seunit, dengan pelaburan minimum RM100 dan maksimum RM1 juta. “Langganan boleh dibuat melalui cawangan pengedar yang sah di seluruh negara, iaitu Malayan Banking Bhd (Maybank), AmBank Bhd, AmBank Islamic Bhd, Bank Islam Malaysia Bhd dan Bank Kerjasama Rakyat Malaysia Bhd,” katanya. – BERNAMA

title: 'Mahkamah Tinggi kekalkan anugerah RM77 juta kepada kontraktor utama Menara Merdeka
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR: Mahkamah Tinggi mengekalkan keputusan Tribunal Timbang Tara menganugerahkan RM77 juta kepada kontraktor utama Menara Merdeka Maybank (sebelum ini dikenali Menara Merdeka 118) . Keputusan tribunal menghendaki Global Wall (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd (GWM) membayar RM77,022,327.67 kepada Samsung C&T Corporation UEM Construction JV Sdn Bhd (SUJV) membabitkan pertikaian kerja fasad bagi projek mercu tanda berkenaan. Pesuruhjaya Kehakiman, Rajes Raghavuji menolak permohonan GWM mencabar keputusan itu, dengan memutuskan isu dibangkitkan sama ada secara individu atau kumulatif, gagal melepasi syarat bagi membolehkan keputusan tribunal diketepikan mengikut Akta Timbang Tara. GWM mencabar keputusan tribunal dengan alasan, antaranya melampaui bidang kuasa, pelanggaran keadilan semula jadi, kegagalan menimbangkan bukti dan hujah, tuntutan lanjutan masa dan kehilangan keuntungan. Rajes berkata, alasan itu secara intipatinya, adalah ketidaksepakatan terhadap dapatan fakta tribunal, keutamaan keterangan, dan tafsiran serta pemakaian undang-undang dan subkontrak oleh tribunal. Pertikaian timbul selepas GWM dilantik menjalankan kerja subkontrak fasad bagi pembangunan Merdeka 118. GWM menggantung kerja subkontrak pada 27 Oktober 2022, manakala SUJV kemudiannya menamatkan subkontrak berkenaan pada 18 Februari 2023. Perkara itu kemudiannya dirujuk kepada tribunal di hadapan tiga anggota terdiri daripada Ian Pennicott KC SC, Richard Wilmot-Smith KC dan David Bateson. Tribunal mendapati, kerja penggantungan kerja oleh GWM sah mengikut undang-undang, manakala penamatan subkontrak oleh SUJV adalah tidak sah. Bagaimanapun, selepas menentukan tuntutan dan tuntutan balas setiap pihak, tribunal memerintahkan GWM membayar RM77,022,327.67 kepada SUJV, faedah RM4,939,123.37 sehingga 16 Disember 2025, dengan faedah lanjut RM14,111.78 sehari dari 17 Disember 2025 sehingga pembayarannya diselesaikan. Anugerah kos berasingan memperuntukkan, 75 peratus daripada kos timbang tara memihak kepada SUJV. GWM menghujahkan, keputusan tidak munasabah kerana tribunal mendapati penamatan oleh SUJV tidak sah, namun masih memerintahkannya membayar lebih RM77 juta. Bagaimanapun, Rajes menolak hujahan itu, dengan menyatakan isu penamatan hanya satu daripada pelbagai isu dikemukakan di hadapan tribunal bagi penentuan. "Dapatan tribunal mengenai isu itu yang memihak kepada GWM tidak dengan sendirinya, menghalang SUJV daripada berjaya dalam isu bebas yang lain," katanya dalam alasan penghakiman diterbitkan Jabatan Kehakiman semalam. Rajes berkata, komponen tunggal terbesar dianugerahkan kepada SUJV ialah ganti rugi kelewatan RM33,561,503.39, yang timbul daripada kegagalan GWM menyiapkannya kerja mengikut tarikh siap yang dilanjutkan. Beliau turut mengambil perhatian, bahawa faedah RM9,691,621.22 timbul daripada pembalikan keputusan adjudikasi, manakala caj balik dan item pengambilalihan berpunca daripada dapatan ke atas tanggungjawab bagi kerja tertentu. Mahkamah juga menolak percubaan GWM untuk bersandar kepada kesan kumulatif aduannya. Rajes berkata, bilangan aduan tidak mengubah sifatnya yang, secara intipati, adalah cabaran terhadap merit keputusan tribunal. Beliau berkata pihak-pihak sendiri memilih untuk membiarkan pertikaian mereka ditentukan panel tiga penimbang tara berpengalaman. Peguam Darshendev Singh dan Michelle Yap mewakili GWM, manakala Harold Tan, Serene Hiew dan Tan Joon Meng bertindak bagi pihak SUJV.
