body: 'KUALA LUMPUR 8 Sept — Kontrak bekalan elektrik baharu yang diperoleh MN Holdings Berhad bagi pelanggan sektor semikonduktor berpotensi menjadi petunjuk awal kepada kitaran perbelanjaan modal (capex) baharu dalam industri tersebut, menurut Maybank Investment Bank (Maybank IB). Tambah firma itu, perkembangan berkenaan dilihat positif kerana permintaan terhadap infrastruktur bekalan tenaga dijangka meningkat seiring dengan pengembangan kapasiti dan pelaburan baharu pemain industri semikonduktor. Ia merujuk kejayaan kumpulan tersebut baru-baru ini memperoleh kontrak daripada Tenaga Nasional Berhad (TNB) bagi pemasangan kabel bawah tanah 275kV baharu untuk sambungan ke Intel Electronic Malaysia di Pulau Pinang. "Kontrak bernilai RM67.3 juta itu diperoleh MN Holdings bersama Pembinaan Tajri Sdn Bhd (PTSB) menerusi konsortium usaha sama (JV) dengan pegangan 80:20, dan berdasarkan pegangan itu, nilai efektif projek kepada kumpulan adalah RM53.9 juta," kata Maybank IB. Tender bekalan tenaga baharu ujar firma penyelidikan tersebut, terutama untuk pelanggan semikonduktor berpotensi menandakan permulaan semula kitaran capex dalam sektor semikonduktor, dengan tempoh pelaksanaan projek adalah selama 18 bulan. Ia dijangka siap pada separuh pertama 2028 dengan andaian margin keuntungan selepas cukai (PAT) sebanyak 7% bagi projek TNB, kontrak berkenaan dianggarkan menyumbang sekitar *RM3.7 juta kepada PAT MN Holdings sepanjang FY27 hingga FY28. Tambah Maybank IB, kontrak tersebut bukan sahaja menambah buku tempahan, malah memberi isyarat bahawa pelaburan infrastruktur berkaitan semikonduktor mungkin kembali meningkat selepas tempoh lebih berhati-hati dalam perbelanjaan modal. "Keperluan terhadap bekalan elektrik yang stabil dan berkapasiti tinggi merupakan komponen penting bagi operasi kemudahan pembuatan semikonduktor, khususnya apabila pengeluar meningkatkan kapasiti pengeluaran dan membangunkan fasiliti baharu," katanya. Justeru, peningkatan pelaburan dalam sektor berkenaan dijangka memberi manfaat kepada pemain kejuruteraan mekanikal dan elektrik (MEP) seperti MN Holdings yang mempunyai kepakaran dalam infrastruktur tenaga. Kumpulan itu ujar Maybank IB, turut mempunyai pendedahan kukuh kepada projek berkaitan pusat data (DC) dan TNB, menjadikannya antara penerima manfaat utama daripada peningkatan permintaan terhadap infrastruktur tenaga. Sementara itu, kemenangan kontrak terbaharu meningkatkan jumlah kontrak baharu bagi FY27 setakat tahun ini kepada RM288.4 juta, bersamaan 24% daripada sasaran pengisian semula buku tempahan FY27 sebanyak RM1.2 bilion. Buku tempahan terkumpul MN Holdings kini meningkat kepada RM1.7 bilion, memberikan perlindungan hasil sekitar 1.9 kali ganda berdasarkan hasil FY26. "Kami turut melihat momentum pemberian kontrak TNB semakin rancak, dengan tender berkaitan TNB merangkumi 54% daripada buku tender kumpulan ini bernilai RM5 bilion, dan penganugerahan ini dilihat positif kerana ia menunjukkan peningkatan dalam pelaksanaan projek TNB,” katanya. Firma penyelidikan itu mengekalkan unjuran pendapatan MN Holdings kerana kontrak berkenaan telah diambil kira dalam andaian pengisian semula buku tempahan FY27 sebanyak RM1.2 bilion. Maybank IB turut mengekalkan saranan 'beli' dengan harga sasaran (TP) RM4.19 sesaham, berdasarkan nisbah harga kepada pendapatan (P/E) FY27E sebanyak 21 kali. Ujarnya, MN Holdings kekal sebagai pilihan utama firma penyelidikan dalam sektor MEP, disokong kedudukan kukuhnya dalam projek infrastruktur tenaga untuk pusat data dan TNB. Dengan prospek pemulihan capex semikonduktor, momentum projek TNB yang semakin rancak serta buku pesanan RM1.7 bilion, MNH dilihat berada pada kedudukan baik untuk menikmati pertumbuhan pendapatan dalam tempoh beberapa tahun akan datang.

title: 'Maybank terima kelulusan BNM ambil alih baki pegangan Etiqa RM4.83 bilion | DagangNews - Berita Bisnes Anda
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR 8 Sept - Malayan Banking Bhd (Maybank) menerima kelulusan Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) pada 1 September 2026 untuk mengambil alih baki 30.95% pegangan dalam syarikat induk Etiqa daripada syarikat insurans Belgium, Ageas SA, pada harga RM4.83 bilion. Dalam makluman kepada Bursa Malaysia, Maybank berkata, susulan kelulusan itu pihaknya telah memeterai perjanjian jual beli saham tanpa syarat dengan Ageas Insurance International NV dan Ageas SA/NV bagi pengambilalihan baki kepentingan dalam Maybank Ageas Holdings Bhd (MAHB). Urus niaga itu, yang pertama kali diumumkan pada 3 Ogos lalu, akan dibiayai sepenuhnya menerusi dana yang dijana secara dalaman oleh Maybank. Selepas pengambilalihan selesai, Maybank akan memiliki 100% MAHB, sekali gus memberikan kumpulan perbankan itu kawalan penuh terhadap perniagaan insurans dan takaful Etiqa di Malaysia dan Singapura. MAHB kini merupakan anak syarikat Maybank dengan pegangan sebanyak 69.05% menerusi Etiqa International Holdings Sdn Bhd (EIHSB). MAHB berfungsi sebagai syarikat pegangan bagi perniagaan insurans dan takaful Etiqa di Malaysia dan Singapura, yang menawarkan produk insurans hayat dan am konvensional serta produk takaful keluarga dan am melalui pelbagai saluran pengedaran. Maybank berkata pemilikan penuh MAHB akan memberikan fleksibiliti strategik lebih besar kepada kumpulan untuk mempercepat inovasi produk, memperluas penembusan bankasurans, mengembangkan tawaran takaful serta meningkatkan kecekapan modal dan operasi dalam perniagaan insurans dan takaful. Harga pembelian RM4.83 bilion itu, selepas mengambil kira dividen RM800 juta yang akan dibayar oleh MAHB pada tarikh penyelesaian, mewakili penilaian sebanyak 1.98 kali nilai buku dan 15.3 kali pendapatan. Di bawah urus niaga tersebut, Ageas akan menerima RM248 juta daripada dividen berkenaan, manakala Maybank menerusi EIHSB akan menerima RM552 juta. Urus niaga itu dijangka diselesaikan pada 11 September 2026. Selepas penyelesaian, aset bersih sesaham Maybank dijangka menurun kepada 7.19 sen daripada 7.73 sen pada akhir Disember 2025. Jumlah pinjaman pula dijangka meningkat kepada RM45.54 bilion daripada RM44.24 bilion, manakala nisbah gearing meningkat kepada 0.52 kali berbanding 0.47 kali sebelumnya. Pengambilalihan itu merupakan sebahagian daripada strategi Maybank untuk memperkukuh perniagaan insurans dan takaful Etiqa, termasuk memperdalam penembusan pelanggan, mempercepat pengembangan serantau serta meningkatkan kecekapan pengurusan modal.

body: 'Other achievements include Best Company in IR by Sector, Best Financial Reporting and Best CEO in IR Maybank, one of ASEAN’s leading financial services institutions, achieved a landmark recognition at Bursa Malaysia’s inaugural Investor Relations Awards 2026, securing four awards across company and leadership categories. The recognition reflects Maybank’s focus on long term shareholder value and the role of investor relations in advocating trust, transparency and market confidence, in line with Malaysia’s broader MYValueUp agenda. Leading the Group’s achievements is its recognition as Best Company in IR (Overall), setting a strong standard for investor relations excellence. It highlights Maybank’s clear equity story and consistent engagements with its stakeholders, underpinned by a strong track record of delivery. Maybank wins Best Company at Bursa Malaysia Investor Relations Awards 2026 Supporting this track record, Maybank’s investor relations function is positioned as a strategic role that connects the Group’s strategy, performance and value creation priorities with the expectations of the investment community. This two-way engagement enables investors to gain greater clarity on Maybank’s strategic direction, while helping management remain cognisant of shareholder expectations. At the sectoral level, Maybank was recognised as Best Company in IR by Sector (Large Cap). As Bursa Malaysia’s largest listed company and the nation's largest financial institution, Maybank recognises its responsibility to uphold high standards of market accessibility and investor engagement. This is reflected in a structured and differentiated engagement model, which includes thematic Investor Days, quarterly briefings, non‑deal roadshows, investor conferences and targeted sessions; enabling sustained dialogue and deeper understanding of the Group’s strategy, performance and outlook. Maybank also took home Best Financial Reporting, affirming its commitment to clarity, depth and consistency of its disclosures, going beyond mandatory filings to provide clear, data‑driven insights that support informed investor and analyst decision making. The Group’s integrated reporting suites provided a comprehensive view of financial performance, business drivers, capital and liquidity position, asset quality, dividends and outlook. Maybank’s reporting touchpoints from annual reports to quarterly materials and Annual General Meeting (AGM) disclosures set a benchmark for quality and transparency. Meanwhile, Dato’ Sri Khairussaleh Ramli, President & Group CEO of Maybank was named Best CEO in IR, recognising his leadership, in articulating a clear strategic vision, maintaining active stakeholder engagement and reinforcing market confidence through consistent execution. The award also reflects his role in driving leadership accountability and market accessibility, supported by the Board, senior management and Maybankers. Dato’ Sri Khairussaleh named Best CEO in IR at Bursa Malaysia Investor Relations Awards 2026 “These recognitions belong to all Maybankers. They reflect the discipline, resilience, and commitment of Maybankers in promoting open, consistent, and engaging conversations with the investment community that help build trust as we continue our journey to deliver sustainable shareholder value over the decades. As we execute ROAR30 and support the aspirations of MYValueUp, we remain focused on strengthening market confidence, enhancing investability and delivering long term value through disciplined execution, while ensuring our growth translates into impactful outcomes for all stakeholders,” said Dato’ Sri Khairussaleh Ramli.

title: 'Maybank emerges as top winner at inaugural Bursa Malaysia IR Awards 2026
body:
'

KUALA LUMPUR (Sept 7): Malayan Banking Bhd (KL:MAYBANK) emerged as the biggest winner at the inaugural Bursa Malaysia IR Awards 2026 that was held last Friday, sweeping home three awards including Best Financial Reporting and the flagship Best Company in IR.

Capping the hattrick win for the company was its sectoral win as Best Large-Cap company in IR for Financial Services while its president and group chief executive officer Datuk Seri Khairussaleh Ramli was named Best CEO in IR.

The awards honoured a total of 32 winners across eight main categories, celebrating public listed companies (PLCs) and investor relations professionals who have demonstrated a strong commitment to investor engagement, market communication and corporate transparency, Bursa said in a statement on Monday.

The eight categories are:

  1. Best Company in IR (overall)
  2. Best Financial Reporting
  3. Best Sustainability Communications
  4. Best IPO Company in IR
  5. Best CEO in IR
  6. Best CFO in IR
  7. Best Large-cap Company in IR by Sector (across 13 sectors)
  8. Best Mid/Small-cap Company in IR by Sector (across 13 sectors)

Other notable winners include Tenaga Nasional Bhd (KL:TENAGA), which took home twin awards for Best Sustainability Communications and Best Large-cap Company in IR for Utilities, and Oriental Kopi Holdings Bhd (KL:KOPI), which was named Best IPO Company in IR. 

The other individual award — the Best CFO in IR — went to Malkit Singh Maan of Hong Leong Bank Bhd (KL:HLBANK).

Effective investor relations is important in strengthening the quality and competitiveness of Malaysia's listed companies, said Treasury secretary general Tan Sri Johan Mahmood Merican when delivering the keynote address at the awards celebrations.

“By communicating openly and consistently with investors, public listed companies enable better-informed investment decisions and demonstrate their commitment to transparency and accountability. As we continue enhancing the competitiveness and quality of Malaysia’s listed companies, effective investor engagement will remain an enabler of long-term value creation and sustainable market growth,” Johan said.

The inaugural awards aimed to recognise companies and professionals who are setting a high standard for transparency, engagement and market communication, said Bursa CEO Datuk Fad'l Mohamed.

"By spotlighting these practices, we hope to encourage more listed companies to strengthen their investor relations capabilities and help raise standards of investor engagement across the market," he said.

He also noted that there is considerable opportunity to strengthen IR capabilities across the market and enhance issuer-investor engagement across the market.

Based on Bursa's research, only 32% of listed companies have a dedicated internal IR function while 17% outsource the function and 51% operate without any formal IR structure.

The exchange operator and regulator said it has been building IR capabilities in the capital market through IR4U by providing practical guidance and learning opportunities for PLCs, which saw the participation of about 690 listed companies throughout 2024 and 2025.

These efforts are complemented by MY Value Up, the national capital market initiative jointly launched by the Securities Commission Malaysia and Bursa to encourage companies to strengthen fundamentals while articulating their strategies and priorities more clearly to the market.

The complete list of award winners will be featured in a special pullout in The Edge Malaysia weekly.

Pengerusi PAWE Kuala Kubu Bharu Shamsul Akhyar Abdullah berkata program berkenaan bukan sekadar aktiviti tanggungjawab sosial korporat (CSR), malah mencerminkan keprihatinan dan penghargaan terhadap golongan warga emas. “Program seperti ini bukan sekadar satu aktiviti CSR, tetapi merupakan satu bentuk keprihatinan, penghargaan dan kasih sayang kepada golongan warga emas. “Inisiatif yang dilaksanakan Maybank membuktikan organisasi korporat bukan sahaja cemerlang dalam bidang perbankan, tetapi turut mempunyai jiwa dan tanggungjawab terhadap masyarakat,” katanya ketika berucap pada majlis berkenaan. Menurut beliau, penglibatan pihak korporat bersama warga emas turut memberi nilai tambah kepada usaha PAWE menyediakan ruang yang lebih aktif, sihat dan bermakna kepada ahlinya. Program berkenaan dirasmikan oleh Ketua Penolong Pegawai Daerah merangkap Pengerusi Jawatankuasa Pembangunan Warga Emas Daerah Hulu Selangor, Mohamad Marwan Ahmad Tajuri. Turut hadir Ketua Perbankan Pengguna Maybank Sukhbir Singh, Ketua Prestasi Perniagaan dan Produktiviti, Zon Sri Damansara Khairulnizam Yusof serta Pengurus Cawangan Maybank Kuala Kubu Bharu Mohd Sabri Ahmad. Dalam perkembangan sama, Maybank turut menyumbangkan dua set kerusi batu marmar kepada PAWE Kuala Kubu Bharu untuk kegunaan ahli-ahli pusat berkenaan. title: 'Maybank raises Malaysia and ASEAN-6 growth forecasts as Invest ASEAN 2026 opens in Singapore
body: 'Around 200 institutional investors are gathering in Singapore for Maybank's flagship Invest ASEAN conference, as the bank lifts its 2026 GDP growth outlook for Malaysia and the wider ASEAN-6 region. Around 200 institutional investors and prime brokerage clients with a combined $23 trillion (MYR93 trillion) in global assets under management are convening at Maybank Investment Banking Group's ("Maybank IBG") flagship event, Invest ASEAN, on 7-8 July in Singapore. The event connects investors with 54 companies including a sovereign wealth fund, alongside meetings with key government bodies in Singapore. The companies are from ASEAN-6 markets (Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia, the Philippines and Vietnam) and India, representing total market capitalisation of $553 billion. Spanning banking, technology, consumer, healthcare, manufacturing and renewable energy sectors, the companies were selected based on clients' preferred names, a mix of mid and large caps, readiness to engage with global investors and Maybank IBG's research views. Michael Oh-Lau, chief executive officer, Maybank Investment Banking Group said, "Now in its 13th edition, Invest ASEAN reinforces Maybank's long-standing commitment to connecting investors with companies while providing the insights and conviction needed to navigate today's evolving global landscape. This year's attendance surpassed our expectations, highlighting sustained interest from both global and local investors in ASEAN as the region continues to demonstrate resilience amid global uncertainties. Energy transition, supply chain reconfiguration and AI-led digital transformation are key themes at this year's Invest ASEAN, and we expect these trends to continue over the next few years." Reflecting improved conditions, Maybank's research has revised its ASEAN-6 GDP growth forecast upwards to +4.7% from its estimate of +4.5% in March (2027E: +4.7%). Oil prices have fallen from their peak to near pre-war levels and tanker traffic via the Strait of Hormuz is recovering. In Malaysia, Maybank has revised its full-year 2026 GDP growth forecast upwards to 4.9% from 4.4%, reflecting resilient economic momentum in the first half of the year despite the heightened geopolitical risks. Economic indicators for April and May point to another quarter of growth above 5%, underpinned by robust manufacturing activities and stronger net exports as Malaysia benefits from the AI-driven technology upcycle, and being a net energy exporter amid higher commodity prices. Outlook for the second half of 2026 remains healthy, especially amid the sustained momentum in investment approvals, particularly in technology, renewable energy, industrial real estate and infrastructure segments. Maybank also remains positive on the market, with a year-end FBM KLCI target of 1,750 based on 7.5% earnings growth, sustained investment upcycle effects, stable consumer essentials spending and steady foreign participation. The expansion of KLCI to 50 constituents, from 30 currently, promises to reinvigorate broader sectoral picks whilst benefitting from the momentum of the MY Value Up initiative. As AI and data centre themes take centre stage, Maybank has upgraded its view on the technology sector, which is expected to benefit from these long-term structural growth drivers. title: 'Felda’s Road Ahead in the Spotlight
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 6): Seven years after Malaysians were made aware of the problems confronting the Federal Land Development Authority (Felda), the institution is once again at a crossroads. Felda, which has the largest plantation footprint in the country and has helped improve the livelihoods of more than 100,000 original settlers and their families, is undergoing another strategic review amid concerns over its long-term sustainability. An interim report on the Felda Group Strategic Roadmap 2025-2030 (HTF 30) was submitted last month by the Special Committee on the Strategic Plan for Felda Group to Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim. Among the proposals under consideration is a redefinition of Felda’s mandate, including a review of the Land Development Act that governs the agency, as the committee monitors actions taken following the 2019 Felda White Paper, according to people with knowledge of the matter. The review comes as the highly indebted entity grapples with crucial replanting costs that could reach RM900 million annually, on top of more than RM900 million in financing costs currently borne by the government. Felda oversees some 870,000ha of land, of which 490,000ha was allocated to settlers, 330,000ha to Felda’s commercial plantations — later placed under FGV Holdings Bhd — and another 50,000ha for village development. Fragmented and ineffective management of the land and operations, together with questionable transactions and investments, resulted in heavy losses despite Felda receiving billions of ringgit from the listing of its commercial arm, then known as Felda Global Ventures Holdings Bhd. By 2017, Felda’s borrowings had ballooned to RM12.1 billion from just RM100 million in 2007. In 2023, the government guaranteed and agreed to service Felda’s RM9.9 billion sukuk, issued to fund the RM3.7 billion privatisation of FGV to consolidate its estate operations, as well as Felda and settlers’ debt. But more needs to be done before those efforts bear fruit. In 2012, Felda raised RM6 billion through the offer for sale of FGV shares during the latter’s initial public offering, while FGV itself raised RM4.5 billion from investors. In total, the exercise raised RM10.5 billion. Instead of directing more of those proceeds towards critical needs such as replanting, the 2019 Felda White Paper found that RM4.6 billion, or 76% of Felda’s IPO proceeds, went towards what it described as “unproductive spending”, while another RM1.4 billion was channelled into investments that failed to generate returns. The spending included RM1.69 billion in special payments to settlers, RM550 million in one-off contributions to state governments, RM400 million in loans for settlers’ house extensions, RM406 million to redeem FGV shares and RM177 million in listing expenses. FGV, meanwhile, spent RM3.3 billion, or 73% of its RM4.5 billion in IPO proceeds, on investments and developments that did not generate satisfactory returns. FGV, which leased Felda’s plantation land, also failed to achieve the yields Felda had projected, leaving the agency with an earnings shortfall. Following FGV’s privatisation, Felda is looking at consolidating the management of its commercial estates and settlers’ land. But that alone will not resolve the underlying balance-sheet problem, particularly the heavy capital requirements needed to keep the estates productive. Beyond its plantation operations, Felda bears significant social obligations to settlers, including spending on housing, infrastructure and income support for up to five years during the replanting cycle. Today, the families of Felda settlers span as many as six generations and number about 2.8 million people. In many respects, Felda has fulfilled its original mandate of opening up rural land and developing communities alongside settlers, about 95% of whom have received titles to their land. Without a clear framework for its future model, the institution’s role and the financial obligations that come with it risk continuing to be shaped by factors beyond its core mandate, particularly when political considerations intersect with policy during periods of adjustment. Any new roadmap will therefore have to define more clearly where Felda’s commercial responsibilities end and its social obligations begin, and how each should be funded. Felda was in better shape before the mismanagement that followed the windfall from FGV’s listing, when the institution was earning around RM3 billion a year. There are also arguments that greater provisions should have been made for replanting, which is central to sustaining its core operations. Poor investment decisions, however, turned Felda’s fortunes upside down in less than a decade. A forensic audit found RM2.2 billion in asset impairments from eight transactions undertaken by Felda and Felda Investment Corporation Sdn Bhd (FIC) between 2010 and 2018 — equivalent to half of their initial RM4.4 billion investment value. Among them were PT Eagle High Plantations Tbk, the Kuala Lumpur Vertical City (KLVC) project and several London properties. One of the largest was Felda’s US$505.4 million acquisition of a 37% non-controlling stake in Eagle High Plantations in 2016 at a premium, resulting in an impairment loss of RM1.576 billion in 2017. Its London property purchases also came under scrutiny over discrepancies between reported acquisition prices and amounts received by vendors, while some properties saw their values fall sharply soon after acquisition. KLVC, meanwhile, remains the subject of a legal dispute between Felda and developer Synergy Promenade Sdn Bhd (SPSB) over the development of Felda land along Jalan Semarak. Former FIC chief executive officer Mohd Zaid Abdul Jalil has also been charged with two counts of cheating the company’s board, which allegedly resulted in the ownership of 16 land parcels being transferred from Felda to SPSB. Source: TheEdge - 6 Oct 2026

title: 'Govt Dividend Receipts Up 1.4% to RM39.55b in 2025 on Higher BNM, Khazanah Payouts — AG’s Report
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 5): The federal government received RM39.55 billion in dividends from its investments in 2025, up by 1.4% from RM39.01 billion a year earlier, as higher payouts from Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) and Khazanah Nasional Bhd outweighed lower receipts from other entities. The dividends came from 20 companies and two statutory bodies, compared with 21 companies and two statutory bodies in 2024. The increase was RM535.06 million compared to last year, according to the latest auditor general’s report released on Monday. Petroliam Nasional Bhd (PETRONAS) paid RM32 billion, unchanged from 2024. BNM paid RM5.25 billion, up from RM2.85 billion, an increase of RM2.4 billion or 84.2%. Khazanah's dividend doubled to RM2 billion from RM1 billion. Bank Simpanan Nasional paid RM25 million, down from RM52 million. Dividends from statutory bodies rose 81.8% to RM5.28 billion, while those from companies fell 5.1% to RM34.27 billion. In all, nine companies and one statutory body paid RM7.43 billion, against RM3.98 billion in 2024, an increase of RM3.45 billion or 86.7%. Twelve companies and one statutory body paid less compared to 2024, as three companies paid the same amount in both years. Piramid Pertama Sdn Bhd, which paid RM2.73 billion in 2024, made no payment in 2025. Dividends from Prokhas Sdn Bhd fell to RM5.6 million from RM56.24 million. Three companies, Perbadanan Nasional Bhd, Malaysia Debt Ventures Bhd and Malaysia Digital Economy Corp Sdn Bhd paid dividends in 2025 after paying none in 2024. Source: TheEdge - 6 Oct 2026

title: 'Private Deal: Celebrity-founded nasi padang restaurant chain Bumbu Babah aims to raise RM20 mil
body: 'Private Deal: Celebrity-founded nasi padang restaurant chain Bumbu Babah aims to raise RM20 mil This article first appeared in Wealth, The Edge Malaysia Weekly on September 28, 2026 - October 4, 2026 Transitioning from the entertainment industry to the food and beverage (F&B) sector is not easy, but when comedian Ajak Shiro heard his child express a desire to start a fried chicken business, he thought of making the idea a reality. Ajak, whose real name is Mohd Hanaffi Razak, looked for a business partner. This ended up being Aliey Othman, an F&B industry veteran with 20 years of experience and involvement in many notable brands. Starting with fried chicken as the foundation, their conversation gradually evolved into a discussion on nasi padang, a Minangkabau meal of steamed rice and a variety of side dishes. “In Malaysia, nasi padang hasn’t become mainstream yet. Moreover, it is considered expensive, so we thought of coming up with a large-scale nasi padang brand, but with low prices,” says Ajak. He went on to start Babah Ventures Sdn Bhd (BBV) and opened its first stall, named Bumbu Babah, at a food court in Giant Batu Caves in November 2024. There are now more than 50 outlets across Peninsular Malaysia and the company is on track to reaching 60 outlets this year. Delivering affordable and accessible food is important to Ajak. So, a plate of nasi padang can be priced as low as RM9.90. The uncompromised value the company offers in terms of price point and flavour has become Bumbu Babah’s unique selling point, he says. “At this time, we understand the current economic situation. If we look at the customers now, they value the experience of eating in restaurants more, they like good food, but they’re quite sensitive to price,” says Ajak. To accelerate its next stage of growth, BBV will launch an equity crowdfunding (ECF) campaign on pitchIN to attract institutional investors with its numbers, create a fundraising exercise with customer engagement and possibly look at fast-tracking to an initial public offering (IPO) by 2028 at the earliest. On the ECF platform itself, the company aims to raise between RM5 million and RM20 million, with shares issued at RM10 each. BBV plans to allocate 40% of the funds from the ECF campaign to acquiring its top-performing licensed outlets. Two activities, the setting up of corporate-owned outlets in malls and supporting the rollout of the new concept, will be allocated 25% each, while the final 10% will go to enhancing technology and its working capital. Behind the quick expansion The business has been able to expand quickly because its licensees have shown interest in opening more outlets. “We call it a licensed-and-managed concept because we are very mindful that we don’t want licensees or franchisees to run the outlets their own way and steer away from the standard operating procedures (SOPs). So, we came up with a structure where they provide the funding and become a passive investor in the outlet,” says BBV corporate finance manager Chan Eu-Jinn. This is how the system works: the licensee fully owns the outlet, but BBV continues to run it as if it belonged to the company. BBV also charges a management fee based on a percentage of the licensed outlet’s earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) on a monthly basis. “If the outlet is not profitable, we do not charge the management fee, so we have to ensure that it is run properly,” he notes. There are currently seven corporate-owned Bumbu Babah outlets. The remaining outlets are owned by licensees. BBV aims to continue expanding, but with a strategy centred more on mall outlets. “Our MyTown, Melawati Mall and IOI City Mall outlets are doing well, but we are still not in a lot of the major malls in the market yet. With the funds raised, we can then invest in this,” says Chan. BBV acknowledges that F&B brands have a tendency to overexpand, and Chan says the company has addressed this by setting a target number of outlets for Bumbu Babah restaurants so as to retain operational quality. “When we hit our target number [we may look more into] maintenance, but we will not be growing for the sake of opening and then cannibalising ourselves.” Bumbu Babah was also able to grow quickly with the introduction of a centralised kitchen to ensure the quality of the food across its licensed outlets remains consistent. Chan says the curry, sambal, proteins and sides are prepared in advance and sent straight to the outlets. This contributes to the efficiency of its operations, as the staff are able to run the basic equipment at the outlets by following the SOPs. Ajak plans to develop more offerings beyond Bumbu Babah’s nasi padang menu. Reflecting this resolve is BBV’s recent collaboration with local music group KRU to open a fine-casual-dining restaurant called KRU Cafe. “We will also have stalls where we will have food menus that include Chinese and Indian food. This is one of the projects that we will implement in time to come, and I think this is one of the reasons why Bumbu Babah will continue to grow in the F&B industry for many more years,” he says. On solid operational and financial ground Based on its audited financial statements, BBV is in a strong financial position. The company has four income streams: retail sales at corporate-owned outlets, central kitchen supplies, monthly management fees and turnkey outlet set-ups involving the building and selling of completed outlets to licensees. For its financial year 2025 (FY2025) ended on Dec 31, the parent company made RM10.4 million in revenue, while the consolidated group revenue came up to RM25.9 million. As for net profit, the parent company recorded RM2.5 million, while the group registered RM3.2 million. This gives the group a net profit margin of 12.5%, which Tradeview Capital research analyst Tan Jia Hui says sits at the higher end of the F&B industry norm of 5% to 12%. “The normalised margin is more likely to settle at around 10% in the upcoming years, given the margin mix [of all four income streams],” she adds. The margin is also anchored by a low marketing spend of roughly 1.3% of its revenue due to the marketing pull of Ajak. The group’s FY2025 earnings quality can be considered clean with only RM24,000 coming from one other source of income, which is the interest from its fixed deposits. Tan notes that liquidity was BBV’s clearest improvement in FY2025, with the current ratio moving from 0.21 times to 1.71 times and the quick ratio from 0.20 times to 1.70 times. Working capital swung from -RM560,000 to RM1.52 million, while its return on assets rose sharply from 6.6% to 74%. The company has also fully repaid shareholder advances in FY2025, leaving the group free of debt or borrowings. “In FY2024, the business leaned on RM600,000 of shareholder and director advances and stretched trade payables to fund itself, so its total liabilities-to-equity ratio stood at 13.9 times. In FY2025, those advances were repaid, so there are no borrowings and no non-current liabilities. The group holds net cash of RM1.47 million, taking the liabilities-to-equity ratio down to 0.97 times,” he says. Gordon Low, founder and managing partner of management consulting firm PiValue Strategy, agrees with Tan. He notes that the company’s financial improvements are backed by positive cash flow rather than being just profit on paper. “This is a company entering its next fundraising round from a position of real financial substance, which is a reasonable and encouraging starting point for the growth questions that follow,” he says. We didn’t want to have an additional delivery business affect our operations. So we’re confident that even with all these challenges, we’re on track to hitting our target this year,” says Chan. title: 'Govt dividend receipts up 1.4% to RM39.55b in 2025 on higher BNM, Khazanah payouts — AG’s report
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 5): The federal government received RM39.55 billion in dividends from its investments in 2025, up by 1.4% from RM39.01 billion a year earlier, as higher payouts from Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) and Khazanah Nasional Bhd outweighed lower receipts from other entities. The dividends came from 20 companies and two statutory bodies, compared with 21 companies and two statutory bodies in 2024. The increase was RM535.06 million compared to last year, according to the latest auditor general’s report released on Monday. Petroliam Nasional Bhd (PETRONAS) paid RM32 billion, unchanged from 2024. BNM paid RM5.25 billion, up from RM2.85 billion, an increase of RM2.4 billion or 84.2%. Khazanah's dividend doubled to RM2 billion from RM1 billion. Bank Simpanan Nasional paid RM25 million, down from RM52 million. Dividends from statutory bodies rose 81.8% to RM5.28 billion, while those from companies fell 5.1% to RM34.27 billion. In all, nine companies and one statutory body paid RM7.43 billion, against RM3.98 billion in 2024, an increase of RM3.45 billion or 86.7%. Twelve companies and one statutory body paid less compared to 2024, as three companies paid the same amount in both years. Piramid Pertama Sdn Bhd, which paid RM2.73 billion in 2024, made no payment in 2025. Dividends from Prokhas Sdn Bhd fell to RM5.6 million from RM56.24 million. Three companies, Perbadanan Nasional Bhd, Malaysia Debt Ventures Bhd and Malaysia Digital Economy Corp Sdn Bhd paid dividends in 2025 after paying none in 2024. title: 'Venture Capital: Cypress Asia launches RM50 mil debut venture fund with New Hoong Fatt as anchor investor
body: 'Venture Capital: Cypress Asia launches RM50 mil debut venture fund with New Hoong Fatt as anchor investor This article first appeared in Wealth, The Edge Malaysia Weekly on September 28, 2026 - October 4, 2026 Two veterans of Malaysia’s start-up and investment ecosystem — entrepreneur and investor Sivapalan Vivekarajah and former Pitch Platforms Sdn Bhd (pitchIN) chief operating officer Xelia Tong — are launching a RM50 million debut venture fund. Main Market-listed automotive replacement-parts manufacturer New Hoong Fatt Holdings Bhd (NHF) (KL:NHFATT) has committed up to RM20 million as its anchor limited partner. The investment will be made through its wholly owned subsidiary Jhi Soon Manufacturing Industries Sdn Bhd, which will subscribe for up to 20 million Class A redeemable preference shares in Cypress Drive Ventures at RM1 each, NHF said in a filing with Bursa Malaysia. Cypress Drive Ventures is the first fund managed by Cypress Asia Sdn Bhd, which was founded by Sivapalan and Tong. It will target technology-driven local businesses at the pre-Series A and Series A stages that are profitable or have a clear path to profitability. Cypress Asia is seeking the remaining RM30 million from family offices and other investors. Investments will range from RM1 million to RM3 million per company. Cypress Asia expects to make five to seven investments initially and build a concentrated portfolio of 10 to 12 companies if the fund reaches its RM50 million target. Depending on the deal, it may lead the round, co-invest with another fund or join an existing group of investors. The fund has a seven-year term, with the option of two successive one-year extensions. Cypress Asia expects to make its first investment in the first quarter of 2027. It plans to hold its first investment committee meeting in November and already has a pipeline of potential deals that will undergo due diligence. The pipeline will draw on the co-founders’ existing networks, including companies from accelerator ScaleUp Malaysia’s portfolio and Sivapalan’s Soonicorn Collective for later-stage technology businesses as well as businesses within the network Tong built at pitchIN, a digital fundraising and investment platform. Sivapalan and Tong worked together at ScaleUp Malaysia, as a senior partner and a managing partner respectively. They invested in 38 companies under the initiative. Sivapalan also launched the Soonicorn Collective’s Titan, a 12-month coaching and execution programme for founders seeking to scale their business towards RM100 million in revenue, in which 18 businesses took part. “We have a network of companies that we can invest in. Because we’ve been in the ecosystem for so long, people trust us,” says Sivapalan, co-managing partner of Cypress Asia. The firm will also source investments through equity crowdfunding platforms and other venture capital firms. The fund is sector-agnostic but will invest only in technology-driven businesses, says Tong, CEO and managing partner of Cypress Asia. Potential areas include electrical and electronics, automotive, digital health and agriculture. “There are certain areas that we don’t touch — highly regulated businesses, those very dependent on state government contracts, businesses that are purely software, such as human resources software, or very e-commerce-driven. Other than that, we’re quite open,” she says. Cypress Asia will look for companies that can grow profitably and reach a listing or acquisition without having to raise money repeatedly. Tong says an investee should ideally need no more than one or two additional funding rounds after Cypress Asia’s investment. “Our investment thesis is to look for companies that already have a profitable business. It doesn’t have to be a lot; it can be a small profit, or at least they should be profitable this year. But they must be able to prove to us that they can be profitable,” says Sivapalan. “We want to take them to RM8 million to RM10 million in profit over a five-year period and then list them on Bursa Malaysia or another exchange. The good thing about getting them to profitability is that they also become interesting for a merger and acquisition, so it serves a dual purpose.” Endorsement from a public listed company NHF became Cypress Drive Ventures’ anchor investor after about 2½ years of discussions with Tong, as the automotive-parts group explored ways to gain exposure to innovation and diversify its sources of income. Tong first came to know the family behind the company through business and start-up networks when she was at Cradle Fund Sdn Bhd. She had previously encouraged a family member involved in running the group to set up a corporate venture capital arm but the proposal was too early for it at the time. The proposal was subsequently presented to NHF’s board of directors two or three times, with the board raising extensive questions as the company was new to venture investing. Tong says the process gave both sides time to understand what they were entering into and helped build trust. Initially, NHF committed RM10 million. When Cypress Asia decided to apply for Jelawang Capital’s Emerging Fund Managers’ Programme at the end of 2024, NHF raised it to RM12 million, which was the amount of private capital Cypress Asia needed to meet the programme’s 20% threshold for a fund of at least RM60 million. In the end, Cypress Asia was not selected for the programme but Tong says NHF proceeded with the investment as its decision was based on the managers’ experience rather than the prospect of matching capital. It later increased its commitment to RM20 million. “We are blessed to have them as our first and anchor investor. They genuinely want to look at the innovation side of things and potentially diversify into other businesses,” says Tong. For NHF, the fund offers potential financial returns and exposure to businesses and technologies beyond its existing network. Tong also sees the commitment as an example of how cash held by profitable listed companies can be put to work in Malaysia’s venture ecosystem. “I think Securities Commission Malaysia has also always been trying to get more private pockets to actually invest in this space, to make investments in venture funds … A lot of companies, especially listed ones, are sitting on a lot of cash, but it is a lazy balance sheet that is not doing anything for the business,” she says. Sivapalan adds: “[NHF] is a main board company, and they are willing to take a chance with us. It gives other people the confidence that they can also take a chance with us.” Experienced investors Sivapalan and Tong say their previous investments and years spent working with founders will shape how they manage the fund. “We have been through the mill. We did not just come out of corporate finance and decide to do this. We have worked with many founders,” he says. Sivapalan has spent close to four decades as an entrepreneur, coach and angel investor. He has personally invested in 16 businesses as an angel investor and also co-founded ScaleUp Malaysia, as well as founded the Soonicorn Collective. Tong had investment roles at Malaysia Debt Ventures Bhd and Cradle Fund, where she was vice-president of investment and headed the Angel Tax Incentive programme. She later became a managing partner at ScaleUp Malaysia and, most recently, chief operating officer of equity crowdfunding platform pitchIN. Both see the venture fund as a continuation of their earlier work. During ScaleUp Malaysia’s first three years, investments were made at a fixed valuation of RM2.5 million. Sivapalan says some stronger companies wanted ScaleUp as an investor but eventually declined its offer as the valuation was deemed too low. A venture fund gives Cypress Asia more flexibility to invest in such companies at a later stage and at valuations that reflect their growth. “After running an accelerator, the natural progression is to move into a venture capital fund. An accelerator cannot offer different valuations to different companies, so we lost those opportunities … Then Xelia said there might be a corporate investor, and Jelawang came along. So, we thought, ‘Let’s give it a try. Let’s try to raise the fund.’” Sivapalan adds that the broader aim is to rebuild confidence in Malaysia’s venture capital industry. “There is very low trust in the VC industry today … If the VC industry cannot prove itself, then you can’t raise money to support start-ups and help them grow. “The VC model can work, and I think we would like to show that we have the right insights, the right model and the right thinking to make this work.” Save by subscribing to us for your print and/or digital copy. So, a plate of nasi padang can be priced as low as RM9.90. The uncompromised value the company offers in terms of price point and flavour has become Bumbu Babah’s unique selling point, he says.  “At this time, we understand the current economic situation. If we look at the customers now, they value the experience of eating in restaurants more, they like good food, but they’re quite sensitive to price,” says Ajak. title: 'Wealth
body: 'This article first appeared in Wealth, The Edge Malaysia Weekly on September 28, 2026 - October 4, 2026  Two veterans of Malaysia’s start-up and investment ecosystem — entrepreneur and investor Sivapalan Vivekarajah and former Pitch Platforms Sdn Bhd (pitchIN) chief operating officer Xelia Tong — are launching a RM50 million debut venture fund.  Main Market-listed automotive replacement-parts manufacturer New Hoong Fatt Holdings Bhd (NHF) (KL: NHFATT) has committed up to RM20 million as its anchor limited partner.  The investment will be made through its wholly owned subsidiary Jhi Soon Manufacturing Industries Sdn Bhd, which will subscribe for up to 20 million Class A redeemable preference shares in Cypress Drive Ventures at RM1 each, NHF said in a filing with Bursa Malaysia.  Cypress Drive Ventures is the first fund managed by Cypress Asia Sdn Bhd, which was founded by Sivapalan and Tong. It will target technology-driven local businesses at the pre-Series A and Series A stages that are profitable or have a clear path to profitability.  Cypress Asia is seeking the remaining RM30 million from family offices and other investors.  Investments will range from RM1 million to RM3 million per company. Cypress Asia expects to make five to seven investments initially and build a concentrated portfolio of 10 to 12 companies if the fund reaches its RM50 million target. Depending on the deal, it may lead the round, co-invest with another fund or join an existing group of investors.  The fund has a seven-year term, with the option of two successive one-year extensions.  Cypress Asia expects to make its first investment in the first quarter of 2027. It plans to hold its first investment committee meeting in November and already has a pipeline of potential deals that will undergo due diligence.  The pipeline will draw on the co-founders’ existing networks, including companies from accelerator ScaleUp Malaysia’s portfolio and Sivapalan’s Soonicorn Collective for later-stage technology businesses as well as businesses within the network Tong built at pitchIN, a digital fundraising and investment platform.  Sivapalan and Tong worked together at ScaleUp Malaysia, as a senior partner and a managing partner respectively. They invested in 38 companies under the initiative.  Sivapalan also launched the Soonicorn Collective’s Titan, a 12-month coaching and execution programme for founders seeking to scale their business towards RM100 million in revenue, in which 18 businesses took part.  “We have a network of companies that we can invest in. Because we’ve been in the ecosystem for so long, people trust us,” says Sivapalan, co-managing partner of Cypress Asia.  The firm will also source investments through equity crowdfunding platforms and other venture capital firms.  The fund is sector-agnostic but will invest only in technology-driven businesses, says Tong, CEO and managing partner of Cypress Asia. Potential areas include electrical and electronics, automotive, digital health and agriculture.  “There are certain areas that we don’t touch — highly regulated businesses, those very dependent on state government contracts, businesses that are purely software, such as human resources software, or very e-commerce-driven. Other than that, we’re quite open,” she says.  Cypress Asia will look for companies that can grow profitably and reach a listing or acquisition without having to raise money repeatedly. Tong says an investee should ideally need no more than one or two additional funding rounds after Cypress Asia’s investment.  “Our investment thesis is to look for companies that already have a profitable business. It doesn’t have to be a lot; it can be a small profit, or at least they should be profitable this year. But they must be able to prove to us that they can be profitable,” says Sivapalan.  “We want to take them to RM8 million to RM10 million in profit over a five-year period and then list them on Bursa Malaysia or another exchange. The good thing about getting them to profitability is that they also become interesting for a merger and acquisition, so it serves a dual purpose.”  Endorsement from a public listed company  NHF became Cypress Drive Ventures’ anchor investor after about 2½ years of discussions with Tong, as the automotive-parts group explored ways to gain exposure to innovation and diversify its sources of income.  Tong first came to know the family behind the company through business and start-up networks when she was at Cradle Fund Sdn Bhd. She had previously encouraged a family member involved in running the group to set up a corporate venture capital arm but the proposal was too early for it at the time.  The proposal was subsequently presented to NHF’s board of directors two or three times, with the board raising extensive questions as the company was new to venture investing. Tong says the process gave both sides time to understand what they were entering into and helped build trust.  Initially, NHF committed RM10 million. When Cypress Asia decided to apply for Jelawang Capital’s Emerging Fund Managers’ Programme at the end of 2024, NHF raised it to RM12 million, which was the amount of private capital Cypress Asia needed to meet the programme’s 20% threshold for a fund of at least RM60 million.  In the end, Cypress Asia was not selected for the programme but Tong says NHF proceeded with the investment as its decision was based on the managers’ experience rather than the prospect of matching capital. It later increased its commitment to RM20 million.  “We are blessed to have them as our first and anchor investor. They genuinely want to look at the innovation side of things and potentially diversify into other businesses,” says Tong.  For NHF, the fund offers potential financial returns and exposure to businesses and technologies beyond its existing network.  Tong also sees the commitment as an example of how cash held by profitable listed companies can be put to work in Malaysia’s venture ecosystem.  “I think Securities Commission Malaysia has also always been trying to get more private pockets to actually invest in this space, to make investments in venture funds … A lot of companies, especially listed ones, are sitting on a lot of cash, but it is a lazy balance sheet that is not doing anything for the business,” she says.  Sivapalan adds: “[NHF] is a main board company, and they are willing to take a chance with us. It gives other people the confidence that they can also take a chance with us.”  Experienced investors  Sivapalan and Tong say their previous investments and years spent working with founders will shape how they manage the fund.  “We have been through the mill. We did not just come out of corporate finance and decide to do this. We have worked with many founders,” he says.  Sivapalan has spent close to four decades as an entrepreneur, coach and angel investor. He has personally invested in 16 businesses as an angel investor and also co-founded ScaleUp Malaysia, as well as founded the Soonicorn Collective.  Tong had investment roles at Malaysia Debt Ventures Bhd and Cradle Fund, where she was vice-president of investment and headed the Angel Tax Incentive programme. She later became a managing partner at ScaleUp Malaysia and, most recently, chief operating officer of equity crowdfunding platform pitchIN.  Both see the venture fund as a continuation of their earlier work. During ScaleUp Malaysia’s first three years, investments were made at a fixed valuation of RM2.5 million. Sivapalan says some stronger companies wanted ScaleUp as an investor but eventually declined its offer as the valuation was deemed too low.  A venture fund gives Cypress Asia more flexibility to invest in such companies at a later stage and at valuations that reflect their growth.  “After running an accelerator, the natural progression is to move into a venture capital fund. An accelerator cannot offer different valuations to different companies, so we lost those opportunities … Then Xelia said there might be a corporate investor, and Jelawang came along. So, we thought, ‘Let’s give it a try. Let’s try to raise the fund.’”  Sivapalan adds that the broader aim is to rebuild confidence in Malaysia’s venture capital industry. “There is very low trust in the VC industry today … If the VC industry cannot prove itself, then you can’t raise money to support start-ups and help them grow.  “The VC model can work, and I think we would like to show that we have the right insights, the right model and the right thinking to make this work.”

title: 'The socialist tinge running through Malay society and politics | Opinion | The Vibes
body: 'By Murray Hunter A CONSISTENT thread of light, humanitarian socialism, the social-democratic and developmental variety, has long run through Malay society and politics in Malaysia. It appears in traditional cultural traits, interpretations of Islamic social ethics, the policies of major Malay parties including UMNO and PAS, and the structure of the modern economy. This form of socialism today is focused on mutual help, social justice, state intervention for equity, and protection of the community, especially the Malay majority. Private ownership, markets and individual enterprise remain, but they operate within a framework of collective responsibility and guided redistribution, through both the New Economic Policy (NEP) and reserved Malay land. Several deep-rooted Malay cultural traits help explain why such ideas found fertile ground throughout Malaya’s contemporary history. Almost forgotten traditions in the traditional kampong, gotong royong was a practical expression of communal cooperation. Villagers regularly came together to build or repair houses, plant and harvest rice, clear drains and paths, maintain the surau or cemetery, and assist with weddings, funerals and other life-cycle events. The familiar proverb “berat sama dipikul, ringan sama dijinjing” captured the expectation that burdens should be shared. More broadly, Malay society has tended to favour communalism rather than strong individualism. Group harmony, collective responsibility, loyalty to kin and community, and the avoidance of open confrontation often take precedence over assertive personal autonomy or pure self-interest. This cultural orientation creates a natural affinity for policies that stress mutual support, shared welfare and the idea that the community’s well-being is more important than unchecked individual gain. This is partly explained by Malaysia’s high power-distance score on widely used cultural dimensions such as those developed by Geert Hofstede. In high power-distance societies, hierarchy is accepted as normal, and people are generally more willing to follow authority without extensive public questioning. Among many Malays, this has historically translated into relatively high deference to traditional leaders, the state, religious figures and those in positions of formal power. When government programmes are presented as serving the uplift of the Malay community, this readiness to accept direction from above has made large-scale state intervention more readily accepted than it might be in strongly individualistic, low power-distance cultures. The combination of communalism and hierarchical acceptance helped legitimise ambitious top-down social and economic programmes. Islamic teachings have reinforced the same outlook for many. Obligatory zakat functions as a structured redistribution of wealth from those with surplus to the poor, the needy, debtors and other designated categories. The duty to care for orphans, widows and the vulnerable, the prohibition of riba (usury), and the repeated Qur’anic emphasis on adl (justice) have been interpreted by some Muslim thinkers as containing important socialist elements. Early PAS leader Burhanuddin al-Helmy explicitly combined Islamist, nationalist and socialist ideas in the struggle against colonialism and inequality. Malaysian sociologist Syed Hussein Alatas, in his work Islam and Socialism, argued that Islam’s principles of anti-exploitation and social justice made it compatible with non-Marxist forms of socialism focused on fairness and community welfare rather than atheistic materialism or the abolition of private property. In formal politics, the pattern is clear. Early Malay leftist and populist groups drew on ideas of uplifting ordinary people (marhaen). Within UMNO, the decisive shift came after the 1969 racial riots under Tun Abdul Razak. Razak, who had been exposed to British Labour Party and Fabian socialist thought during his studies, spoke of a form of “nationalist socialism” suited to a developing multi-ethnic nation. The New Economic Policy (NEP) that followed introduced large-scale state intervention with two main prongs: the eradication of poverty regardless of race, and the restructuring of society so that Malays and other Bumiputera could participate more fully in the modern economy and no longer be identified primarily with subsistence agriculture. This was deliberate social engineering aimed at equity and national unity. Key institutions created or expanded in the Razak era still shape Malaysia today. FELDA (Federal Land Development Authority) organised large-scale land settlement schemes that moved hundreds of thousands of rural Malay families onto new agricultural plots, complete with housing, infrastructure, technical support and a structured pathway out of poverty. It was a classic state-led redistributive and developmental programme. MARA (Majlis Amanah Rakyat) was established to advance Bumiputera participation in education, skills training, business and entrepreneurship through scholarships, loans, commercial ventures and institutional support. Together with other agencies, these bodies embodied the belief that the state had a positive duty to correct economic imbalances and uplift the Malay community through organised collective effort. There was an assumption that those privileged leaders would always take the interests of the people into action. PAS has contributed its own version of this tinge. Although primarily an Islamist party, it has at various times emphasised welfare provision, rural development, anti-elite rhetoric and social justice framed through Islamic ethics. In the states it has governed for long periods, PAS has pursued policies with clear redistributive and protective elements that appeal to lower-income and rural Malays who value collective support and moral economy over pure market outcomes. That is partly the reason PAS has been in government there for a long period of time. Today’s economy is reflective of this history The contemporary Malaysian economy continues to reflect the Razak-era model and retains strong features of a light socialist or developmentalist system. Government-linked companies (GLCs) play a dominant role in strategic sectors. The public bureaucracy remains large and central in directing economic activity, allocating resources and implementing preferential policies. Equity ownership targets, subsidies, public education and housing programmes, and extensive state involvement in the economy persist. FELDA and MARA continue to operate alongside a wider network of agencies dedicated to Bumiputera economic advancement. Markets and private enterprise function, freehold land ownership is secure, and individual initiative is encouraged, yet they operate within a framework of heavy government guidance and redistributive goals aimed at social and ethnic equity. This is a mixed economy with a pronounced interventionist and welfare character. The Malaysian economy is not laissez-faire capitalism, nor is it Soviet-style central planning. The focus has always been practical and humanitarian, aimed at reducing poverty, correcting historical imbalances, fostering mutual support, and using the state as an instrument of community uplift. Cultural communalism, acceptance of hierarchy, Islamic ethics of justice, and the institutional legacy of Tun Razak’s era have all sustained this approach. The light socialist colouring remains one of the quieter but durable features of Malay society and politics. It can be traced from the kampong practices of gotong royong and communalism, through the cultural readiness to accept authoritative direction for the common good, the ethical teachings of Islam on justice and redistribution, the ambitious nation-building of Tun Razak’s time with institutions such as FELDA and MARA, and the continuing role of GLCs and state guidance in today’s economy. Unfortunately, many politicians today appear to have forgotten this deeper aspect of the Malay political psyche. Too often they have become focused primarily upon their own personal wellbeing, status and material advancement rather than the broader communal and redistributive responsibilities that once animated Malay political culture. When the ethic of shared burden and collective uplift is neglected in favour of private gain, the original spirit that helped shape both society and policy risks being hollowed out. Recovering an awareness of that older communal and humanitarian strand may be necessary if Malay politics is to remain connected to the values that long gave it meaning. – September 4, 2026
